This article introduces the 2020 COMET-ATOMIC challenge, the first competition designed to evaluate the integration of commonsense knowledge graphs with neural networks. Participants were tasked with developing models to answer questions based on the ATOMIC (A large-scale commonsense reasoning dataset) graph, which links concepts, events, and actions via both symbolic and neural representations. The evaluation metric was a set of 250k multiple-choice questions covering reasoning types ranging from single-hop to multi-hop. The study details the task definition, the provided baseline results, and a survey of the 11 participating teams' approaches. The winning model achieved a 76.2% accuracy, a significant 20% improvement over the baseline's 58.2%.

The Hi-GAL survey, conducted using the Herschel Space Observatory, targets cold dust within the Milky Way to investigate star formation across various molecular environments. This comprehensive initiative covers three wavelength bands—70, 145, and 250 $\mu$m—across four distinct Galactic regions: Taurus, Ophiuchus, Musca, and Sagittarius. This work details the data processing methods employed for the survey, which were adapted from the standard pipeline used for Herschel's SPIRE instrument. Specific modifications were made to accommodate the survey's extended observation durations and its multi-band capabilities. The described procedures encompass data calibration, the creation of mosaics, and the generation of final products, which include calibrated images, error maps, and data catalogs.

We have conducted high-resolution spectroscopy on 12 stars in the globular cluster NGC 2808, which are believed to belong to the first generation of stars, in order to determine their elemental abundances. By utilizing the Fe I and Fe II spectral lines, we derived precise values for [Fe/H] and $\alpha$/Fe ratios. Our results indicate a significant spread in iron abundances, with a range of approximately 0.25 dex, which aligns with previous findings of a similar magnitude in this cluster. We also observed a notably elevated $\alpha$/Fe ratio of 0.33 $\pm$ 0.04 dex for the most metal-poor stars, a value that remains consistent across the entire stellar population.

"Single file methods are frequently used to investigate anomalous diffusion in systems lacking the ergodicity of Brownian motion. This study analyzes a one-dimensional overdamped particle undergoing single file diffusion with an entropic potential $V(x) = -kT \ln P_0(x)$, where $P_0(x)$ represents the equilibrium probability distribution. We demonstrate that the average first exit time from an arbitrary interval $[0,L]$ is $t_{avg} = \frac{L^2}{2D}$ and that the probability distribution for first exit times follows a stable law with index $\alpha = 1$. Furthermore, we examine particle displacement statistics and show that the root-mean-square displacement scales as $t^{1/2}$ for short times but transitions to $t^{1/4}$ at long times. These findings align with prior research on single file diffusion in the absence of entropic potentials. Additionally, we establish that an initial velocity $v_0$ can modify the average first exit time, and we discuss the implications of these results for the design of single file diffusion experiments."

In classical probability, Bayes' rule is the standard for updating beliefs. This study introduces a quantum extension of this theorem designed for measurements that yield inconsistent results across different trials. The new formulation reveals that quantum Bayesian inference is non-unique and lacks a single closed-form solution. By applying this quantum Bayes' rule, the analysis confirms the internal consistency of result inferences and the validity of retrodictive quantum state updates. Additionally, the work demonstrates that while the standard von Neumann-Lüders rule represents a valid update method, it is not the exclusive one.

This study examines finite-size corrections to the equation of state for strongly interacting matter across the entire temperature range and varying baryon chemical potentials, utilizing a perturbative framework for high temperatures and a lattice QCD approach for lower regimes. The equation of state is expressed as a function of pressure normalized by its infinite-volume limit at a given temperature and chemical potential. We demonstrate that this ratio converges to unity at a rate proportional to $1/V$ in systems of volume $V$, regardless of how the boundary is defined. This behavior stems from the fact that the leading $1/V^3$ correction originates from a quark-loop term, which remains constant regardless of the volume's geometric shape. Consequently, we establish that spherical droplets experience a leading correction of $0.002$ relative to their infinite-volume counterparts. This effect is expected to be even more pronounced in elongated systems. These findings are particularly relevant for describing the equation of state in small nuclei and the quark-gluon plasma droplets produced in relativistic collision experiments.

Let $I^1$ denote the ideal in the mod 2 Steenrod algebra $\mathcal{A}$ that is generated by the basis $\{Sq^i \mid i > 1\}$. For any integer $n > 2$, we demonstrate that the quotient of the cohomology groups $H^*(\mathbb{RP}^{n}; \mathcal{A}/I^1)$ modulo those elements generated by others is non-trivial.

Ultraviolet observations of high-redshift galaxies in the Lyman-alpha region are essential for studying the epoch of reionization. To achieve this, astronomers require narrowband photometry that can isolate Lyman-alpha emission from the overwhelming continuum background. We have developed a filter prototype designed for Lyman-alpha photometry, utilizing a custom glass coating on Schott BG-38. This filter exhibits a peak transmission of 12% at a central wavelength of 363.5 nm and a full-width at half-maximum of 0.42 nm. Testing with simulated spectra indicates that the filter's performance is adequate for both deep photometry and single-season surveys targeting Lyman-alpha emission from high-redshift sources.

This study addresses optimal control challenges in distributed systems characterized by graph symmetry. We propose a novel, fully distributed optimal control scheme that leverages graph filtering to manage these computations. The approach relies on the system's graph symmetry to formulate the dual of the optimal control problem, enabling the proposed method to execute in a decentralized manner by applying simple graph filters. This process involves only local data exchange among neighboring nodes. We demonstrate the convergence of the proposed scheme to the globally optimal control solution and validate its effectiveness through a case study involving distributed system control on a communication graph.

Image retrieval systems typically utilize deep learning to extract features for representing visual content. However, these methods often fail to align with human intuition, as they rely on feature vectors that are opaque and difficult to interpret. We introduce a novel approach called Active Image Indexing, which indexes images using their semantic attributes. By leveraging this transparent indexing scheme, we enable precise and explainable image searches. Furthermore, our system employs an innovative machine learning strategy to automatically derive human-like search queries from user interactions, thereby bridging the gap between automated retrieval results and human expectations.

We introduce a method for authenticating users over additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channels without a pre-shared key. The approach relies on a physical bit generated from a specific user's wireless transmission, which is captured by the server. To prevent spoofing, the server encrypts this physical bit and transmits the encrypted version back to the user; the user then sends the re-encrypted signal to the server. This exchange creates an encrypted physical bit that retains the transmission characteristics unique to that user, effectively serving as a keyless authentication credential. The user's identity is verified by the server by analyzing the statistical profile of this returned signal. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the reliability of the authentication improves as the initial physical bit length increases. Furthermore, numerical results indicate that the system achieves performance comparable to schemes utilizing pre-shared keys, provided the initial bit length remains sufficiently large.

This study presents a flexible local projection method designed to estimate dynamic responses in multivariate time series, addressing both stationary and non-stationary data. The approach offers two primary advantages over standard linear models: it captures non-linear dynamics and allows impulse effects to vary based on the initial state of the system. A key feature of this method is its reliance on unstructured VAR models for smoothing, meaning it imposes no restrictions on dynamic responses regarding impulse timing or magnitude. Consequently, it avoids the common pitfalls associated with relying on the invertibility of impulse response matrices, such as those found in identification strategies like Choleski decomposition. The theoretical analysis confirms that the estimator achieves root-n consistency and asymptotic normality, while numerical simulations demonstrate its robustness in non-linear environments.

The analysis examines the orbital angular momentum of a charge $q$ undergoing uniform rotation within a constant uniform magnetic field, specifically focusing on contributions arising from interaction with the vacuum. It is demonstrated that the quantum vacuum exerts a force on the orbital component of the charge's momentum, with the magnitude of this Casimir momentum scaling as the square of the charge ($q^2$).

Fine-grained named entity typing (FG-NET) entails identifying specific entity categories for predefined classes. Unlike word embeddings, which often fail to capture nuanced semantic differences, tree structures offer an ideal framework for encoding hierarchical syntactic and semantic relationships. Consequently, we introduce a novel approach leveraging hyperbolic representation for FG-NET through two key contributions. First, we define entity types as points within a discrete tree structure and represent them as vectors in discrete hyperbolic space. Second, we propose a continuous hyperbolic representation that models entity types as refined subspaces of coarse-grained categories. Empirical evaluations on three standard benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance.

This paper establishes the upper bounds for the second Hankel determinant $H_2(n,r)$, defined as $H_2(n,r)=\frac{a_n a_{n+r-2}-a_{n+r-1}a_{n-1}}{a_2a_{n+r}}$, within the class $\mathcal{S}$ of univalent functions and the subclass $\mathcal{U}$ of functions with bounded turn. Specifically, for functions in $\mathcal{S}$, the bound is given as $|H_2(n,r)|\leq\frac{1}{12}$. Furthermore, for the class $\mathcal{U}$, the bound is $|H_2(n,r)|\leq\frac{(n+r-3)(n+r-4)}{2(n+r)(n+r+1)}$, with the exception of the cases where $n=2$ or $n=3$, for which the bound is $|H_2(2,r)|\leq\frac{1}{2(r+1)}$ and $|H_2(3,r)|\leq\frac{1}{2(r+1)}$ respectively. These results are sharp.

Load balancing is a vital strategy for cloud computing data centers to ensure efficient resource utilization and maintain high service quality. However, existing solutions often overlook the impact of virtual machine (VM) placement on this balancing process, particularly in scenarios involving VM reservations. This paper introduces "Prepartition," a novel approach designed to enhance load balancing while effectively addressing concurrent VM reservations and dynamic requests. The algorithm operates in two phases: first, it partitions the physical servers into two groups to isolate reservation-based VMs from other VMs; second, it places dynamic request VMs onto the partitioned servers using the "Best Fit" strategy. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques in terms of load balancing and resource efficiency.

We introduce a fixed-point learning architecture designed to predict Nash equilibria in extensive-form games. This network-driven approach optimizes the prediction by targeting the internal fixed-point representations of the solutions. We establish that the method is realizable within the Shapley value framework for two-player games and the Pearce equilibrium for multi-player variants. Additionally, we demonstrate that the model's performance scales linearly with the number of states and actions. Empirical results indicate that this network surpasses existing methods in predicting equilibria for extensive-form games.

This study addresses the estimation of causal effects when treatment is binary and confounders are observed but incomplete. We establish bounds for these effects under a counterfactual independence assumption, which asserts that the potential treatment effect is independent of the actual treatment status given the observed confounders. Our approach employs these bounds to construct a new estimator, which achieves a faster sample complexity rate than previously known methods for selecting confounders via data-driven selection in high-dimensional settings. We demonstrate that this new rate is optimal by proving a lower bound on sample complexity. Furthermore, we show that, with high probability, these bounded causal effects tightly approximate the true causal effects.

This study addresses the challenge of detecting stealthy attacks on linear time-invariant systems, focusing on scenarios where the attack model is unknown. To resolve this uncertainty, we introduce a predictive monitoring framework that utilizes a reduced-order estimator capable of forecasting system behavior. This approach ensures that the false alarm probability remains constant regardless of the specific attack pattern. Furthermore, we demonstrate that under certain conditions, the framework can achieve detection within a finite number of steps even when dealing with completely arbitrary unknown attacks. Finally, we evaluate the proposed method by comparing its sample boundedness and computational efficiency against established techniques in the field.

Document summarization is a critical natural language processing task, yet it remains underdeveloped for Indian languages due to a lack of suitable summarization frameworks. This study addresses this void by introducing GAE-ISumm, an unsupervised graph-based summarization system tailored for Indian languages. The model generates summaries by constructing a document graph where nodes represent sentences and edges reflect their similarity. We further introduce a novel sentence ranking metric, PageRank-based Sentence Importance (PSI), to identify and extract the most significant sentences for inclusion in the final summary.

This text presents an examination of finite s-rings of Krull type, specifically deriving a congruence applicable to their s-ring order and establishing a congruence for the number of isomorphism classes of simple modules over the simple ring s-ring, which is of Krull-type.

This study reports the outcomes of a multi-epoch astrometric campaign utilizing the Gaia Early Data Release 3 (EDR3) to track proper motion changes for five nearby stars (with parallaxes $\pi \gtrsim 100$ mas) that were previously identified as having likely massive, unseen companions. The analysis incorporates Gaia EDR3 astrometry alongside archival data from Hipparcos and Tycho-Gaia DR3. By applying a rigorous Bayesian analysis to these astrometric solutions, we derive updated constraints on the masses and orbital parameters of the hidden companions. Our results indicate that the unseen objects orbiting HD 168423, HD 160302, and HD 162826 possess masses of $1.1 \pm 0.2 M_{\odot}$, $1.1 \pm 0.2 M_{\odot}$, and $1.1 \pm 0.2 M_{\odot}$ respectively, with semi-major axes of $1.1 \pm 0.2$ AU, $1.1 \pm 0.2$ AU, and $1.1 \pm 0.2$ AU respectively. Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) have become a standard tool in machine learning, merging the generative capabilities of generative models with the feature-learning strengths of autoencoders. Their ability to generate realistic data and extract meaningful patterns has spurred numerous research efforts. Nevertheless, VAEs face two primary limitations: the "posterior collapse" issue, where the model neglects informative latent variables, and the "beta-VAE" dilemma, which forces a manual trade-off between learning meaningful latent representations and ensuring a continuous latent space. This study introduces a novel VAE architecture that simultaneously addresses posterior collapse and optimizes the latent space topology. Our approach features a dual-regularization framework consisting of a "regularized regularizer" designed to prevent mode collapse and a "regularized encoder" that enforces a more continuous latent manifold. Empirical evaluations on the MNIST and FashionMNIST datasets demonstrate that our proposed model outperforms existing state-of-the-art VAE variants in both generation quality and data reconstruction fidelity.

The rapid proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) devices has introduced significant security challenges, particularly regarding unauthorized access and data breaches. This paper proposes a novel private blockchain framework designed to enhance the security and confidentiality of IoT-generated data. The solution empowers smart home users to verify device integrity and monitor their operational status in real time. By integrating geolocation capabilities, the system tracks the physical whereabouts of devices to detect anomalies, such as theft or unauthorized relocation. The proposed architecture was validated through a simulation using 100 devices, demonstrating that the network sustains a throughput of 1,000 transactions per second (TPS) while achieving 99.9% accuracy in identifying the two-dimensional coordinates of each device.

This paper introduces a quantization framework for Log-Likelihood Ratio (L-value) handling in Gray-coded modulation schemes. The method employs deep learning-based models to reduce these L-values to a smaller number of bits while maintaining the integrity of the coding structure through quantization. Additionally, we propose a new deep learning-based model designed to minimize the impact of this quantization error on system performance. Simulation results demonstrate that the framework achieves significant reductions in bit usage for both 16-QAM and 64-QAM configurations with negligible degradation in performance.

This study addresses the fundamental challenge of determining whether a directed acyclic graph (DAG) admits a planar upward drawing. In such a representation, edges can be mapped to polygonal chains where every edge ascends, and the layout remains completely planar. Although this specific problem has been unresolved for decades, we advance the field by presenting the initial algorithms capable of deciding DAG upward planarity in near-linear time. Specifically, we offer a data-dependent algorithm running in $O(m + n \log n + p \log p)$ time and an implicit version operating in $O(m + n \log n + p \log n)$, where $m$ represents the edge count, $n$ the node count, and $p$ the number of page constraints involved. Building on this decision capability, we also introduce methods to construct the actual near-linear upward planar layouts. Our approach hinges on a novel characterization of DAGs that possess upward planar embeddings, utilizing two distinct types of constraints: forbidden subgraphs and specific sets of separation pairs.

Crowdsourcing has emerged as a cost-effective method for obtaining large volumes of data and annotations, yet it introduces significant challenges due to the varying levels of competence and reliability found among contributors. This study examines an ensemble modeling strategy designed to address annotator bias and inconsistency within annotation distributions. By leveraging 'human softmax' distributions, this method models individual tendencies toward specific labels, thereby separating genuine annotator uncertainty from subjective bias. The approach was evaluated on a benchmark image classification task using a dataset of 100,000 noisy labels generated by 1,000 crowd workers. Results indicate that the proposed technique effectively isolates uncertainty from bias, yielding cleaner per-annotator distributions. Furthermore, it provides robust estimates of entropy-based metrics for measuring this uncertainty, which are essential for optimizing task design and enhancing prediction accuracy.

A covering array, denoted as $\text{CA}(N, k, t, q)$, is an $N \times k$ matrix with entries selected from $\{1, \dots, q\}$ such that every possible $t$-tuple combination of symbols from $\{1, \dots, q\}$ is contained within at least one of its $t$ columns. In this work, we examine the structural properties of small $\text{CA}(N, k, 2, q)$s. We demonstrate that the set of rows in any minimal-length binary $\text{CA}(N, k, 2, 2)$ is composed entirely of a specific collection of codewords from a linear code. Furthermore, we establish that every minimal $\text{CA}(N, k, 2, q)$ possesses a specific structure relative to a code constructed from the union of two specialized collections. These structural findings enable us to determine the exact values of the minimum length $N$ for many specific pairs of $k$ and $q$.

This study examines nonlocal games where two spatially separated players, Alice and Bob, receive questions from a third party and aim to provide answers that demonstrate a correlation stronger than any classical system could achieve. While nonlocal games utilizing a shared maximally entangled state of infinite dimensions are known to be undecidable, this paper demonstrates that this complexity persists even when the shared entanglement is noisy. Specifically, we prove that determining whether the value of a nonlocal game reaches 1 using a finite amount of entanglement remains undecidable, even if the employed shared state is not maximally entangled. This finding holds true for a broad category of games, including those where the question sets are finite. Additionally, we show that deciding if the game value equals 1 with a finite sub-dimension of a specific finite-dimensional entangled state is also undecidable.

This work partially reproduces the study titled "A Guided Genetic Algorithm for Automated Reproduction of Crash Gambling," performing a dedicated analysis of the evolutionary processes involved in CRDAR and offering an in-depth examination of the parent-to-offspring development within this algorithmic framework.

The superconducting state in cuprates is hypothesized to emerge from the ordering of quantum fluctuations associated with the vortex lattice. While prior research has identified evidence for dimerization within this lattice, a comprehensive theoretical framework remains elusive. This study reports a dimerized vortex lattice observed in La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_{4}$ (with $x=0.12$) using scanning tunneling microscopy. The findings indicate that the unit cell dimensions are consistent with theoretical predictions for a square-square dimerized configuration. Furthermore, the data suggests the presence of further dimerization at lower temperatures, transitioning to a stripe pattern. These observations align with a model proposing that superconductivity in cuprates results from the ordering of these dimerized vortices.

We contend that the substantial anisotropy observed in thermal photon $v_2$ serves as a crucial indicator of the QGP's shear viscosity. This assertion is grounded in the premise that thermal photon $v_2$ originates primarily from QGP thermal radiation, which is significantly modulated by the medium's viscosity. To substantiate this claim, we conducted thermal photon hydrodynamic calculations across a broad spectrum of viscosity values for central Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=2.76$ TeV. Our findings demonstrate a robust correlation between the magnitude of thermal photon $v_2$ and the ratio of shear to energy viscosity ($\eta/s$). Furthermore, by comparing our results with experimental data, we derived an upper limit for the QGP viscosity of $\eta/s < 0.12$.

We investigate ground states of classical Heisenberg models on both triangular and kagome lattices, constrained by an arbitrary positive lower limit for the scalar product of neighboring spins. Our findings indicate that a complete ground state featuring full long-range order emerges when this imposed scalar product exceeds a specific threshold. Furthermore, we establish the existence of regular magnetic configurations that satisfy the model's constraints without reducing the number of degrees of freedom.

Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) serve as the gold standard for evaluating treatment efficacy. In recent years, there has been a surge in large-scale multi-arm trials designed to concurrently assess numerous treatments within a single experiment. However, traditional multiplicity adjustments for error rates often result in diminished statistical power due to overly conservative thresholds. Consequently, there is a growing demand for FDR control methods that can better leverage data while maintaining rigorous error management. This paper introduces TEFDR, a novel procedure for simultaneously testing multiple treatments with FDR control, specifically tailored for large-scale trials. Theoretically, the method guarantees FDR control even when tests exhibit arbitrary dependence. Furthermore, it demonstrates that when treatment effects are independent, the approach achieves optimality under specific FDR criteria. Extensive simulations and an empirical analysis of data from a leading pharmaceutical firm confirm that TEFDR offers superior statistical power compared to existing methods.

The foundational aspects of cosmological inflation are examined, with an emphasis on the dynamics of the inflaton field. Various inflationary scenarios are analyzed through the lens of the slow-roll approximation, and the consequences of inflationary perturbations are explored.

The tensions observed in the precision measurements of the $W$ boson mass and the lepton flavor universality violation in beauty decays can be resolved within a Type-X Two-Higgs-Doublet-Model (2HDM) that extends the Standard Model. This extension incorporates two complex Higgs doublets and remains compatible with the observed $\tau \to \mu \gamma$ constraints. Notably, this framework predicts an enhanced $W$ boson mass and a distinct pattern of lepton flavor universality violation in $\tau$ decays, which can be tested by the LHCb experiment. Furthermore, the model offers a viable explanation for the recently observed $\sim 5\sigma$ discrepancy in the muon anomalous magnetic moment, $a_\mu$, by satisfying experimental bounds on the flavor-changing $\mu \to e \gamma$ process.

Software maintenance and development frequently involve software engineers (SEs) dealing with numerous ambiguities when they select search queries to find specific code concepts. These Concept Location (QL) tasks are often hindered by the initial queries, which may be vague or expressed in multiple ways, leading to ineffective results. To address this, we introduce QUICKAR, a novel approach that automatically suggests improved query formulations for SEs. By leveraging crowd-sourced insights from GitHub, QUICKAR generates query alternatives and ranks them to highlight the most effective options. Our evaluation indicates that this method significantly outperforms existing techniques in generating and recommending queries for concept location.

Entraining represents a fundamental mechanism in human interaction, where individuals unconsciously synchronize their vocal production patterns, such as speech rate and pause duration, with those of their dialogue partners. This phenomenon is particularly prominent in dialogue, yet current research lacks a precise quantifiable metric to gauge the depth of entrainment between speakers. This study introduces an unsupervised, deep neural network-based framework designed to identify and measure entrainment from co-articulated speech data. By leveraging this model, we demonstrate the ability to distinguish between trained and untrained duos, showcasing its utility for analyzing social dynamics and group formation. Furthermore, we examine how an unsupervised learning model can capture the non-linear effects of various experimental parameters on entrainment, thereby offering new insights into the underlying mechanisms of human interaction.

We introduce the release version of the Robotics Center for Spectral Energy Distribution (RCSEDv2), a suite of open-source utilities designed to visualize spectral and imaging data. Designed for accessibility, the platform utilizes web technologies to execute spectral data analysis directly within a web browser, thereby removing the requirement for users to install specialized software. The system offers three distinct operational modes: (1) an image-centric mode that accepts single images or stacks, enabling visual inspection, interactive browsing, and geolocation; (2) a data-centric mode that accepts individual spectra or spectral stacks, supporting both graphical inspection and data download; and (3) a combined mode that overlays images and spectral information simultaneously. The software is hosted at https://rcsed.astro.ubc.ca/ and is available for public use.

Temporal action segmentation involves partitioning an unlabelled video into distinct functional segments. This research presents SSCAP, an unsupervised learning framework designed to parse video content into coherent action segments without requiring any manual annotations. The model utilizes a self-supervised approach to segment videos based on the temporal frequency of action-related visual cues. By employing a self-supervised object detector to identify action-relevant objects and their associated features, the system segments the video timeline according to the co-occurrence patterns of these features. The framework's efficacy is demonstrated through strong performance across multiple benchmarks, yielding state-of-the-art results on the Breakfast and Charades datasets.

This work investigates single-baryon systems containing hidden charm, specifically the $P_c(4450)$ resonance and the $P_c(4380)$, which were observed by the LHCb collaboration in $p$ pbar $\to J/\psi$ p reactions. We propose that these resonances are molecular states composed of the $J^{\rm P}=3/2^-$ and $J^{\rm P}=5/2^-$ baryon-meson configurations, respectively. By analyzing the production of these resonances in $J/\psi$ p collisions, we derive the coupling constants between the resonances and their constituent particles. Furthermore, we calculate the partial decay widths for these decays and compare our findings with LHCb's experimental measurements. The results indicate that the observed production rates and decay patterns are consistent with the resonances being predominantly molecular in nature.

This study introduces a novel inquiry-based technique for delivering conceptual feedback within software testing education, designed to boost student engagement through questioning. The research empirically contrasts this approach with a traditional detailed feedback mechanism by comparing their impacts on engagement levels, conceptual understanding, and student attitudes toward testing concepts. Drawing on data from 102 participants across two distinct groups, the findings indicate that inquiry-based conceptual feedback outperforms detailed feedback in fostering both higher engagement and stronger conceptual grasp, while also generating more positive attitudes toward testing concepts among the students.

Domain adaptation is essential for deploying machine learning models in real-world scenarios where target data distributions differ from training data. This study focuses on a source-free setting where the source domain is inaccessible, and specifically addresses target labeling with incomplete annotation. We introduce a semi-supervised hypothesis transfer framework that leverages a pre-trained source model to perform domain adaptation. By constructing a semi-supervised target model through the transfer of these hypotheses, the method utilizes both labeled and unlabeled data effectively. We assess the quality of this adapted model using a proposed target-specific layer re-initialization technique. Empirical evaluations on two standard datasets demonstrate that the semi-supervised approach significantly outperforms both semi-supervised and unsupervised state-of-the-art methods.

Nuclear propulsion systems have been investigated for decades as a means to shorten travel durations to Mars and other locations within the solar system. While conventional designs utilizing solid fuel rods or liquid fuel channels face limitations in power density and specific power, the gas-core reactor (GCR) concept offers a promising alternative. The GCR operates by igniting a suspended cloud of fissionable fuel at the reactor's center with a plasma temperature exceeding 100 million Kelvin. This configuration ensures that fission events occur primarily outside the dense zone of self-absorbed neutrons, thereby eliminating the need for heavy neutron moderators and significantly boosting specific power output. This review examines the GCR concept, with a particular focus on its application for deep-space propulsion. The discussion covers fundamental principles, historical context, proposed configurations, and associated technical challenges. Furthermore, the paper outlines a proposed experimental roadmap designed to validate the feasibility of GCRs specifically for deep-space propulsion applications.

Neural networks are increasingly utilized in astroparticle physics for simulating detector responses and analyzing experimental data. Yet, standard neural networks often fail to leverage the specific prior knowledge held by domain experts. This study introduces an architecture tailored to embed explicit domain insights, specifically the spatial regions where particle interactions occur. By integrating this constraint, the model achieves superior performance metrics, including higher F1 scores and lower energy resolution uncertainties compared to baseline models, all while utilizing fewer parameters. These findings indicate that hybrid approaches, merging traditional domain-driven techniques with modern machine learning, hold significant promise for advancing astroparticle physics research.

The study of atmospheres surrounding giant exoplanets and brown dwarfs is crucial for understanding the physical and chemical processes within these celestial bodies. A primary obstacle in analyzing their atmospheres is the scarcity of comprehensive spectroscopic data, which hampers the ability to distinguish between different atmospheric compositions. To address this, we introduce the Molecular Absorption Cross-Section Library for Exoplanet Line Emission and Absorption Spectra (EXOPLINES), a comprehensive database designed to support spectroscopic investigations of these atmospheres. EXOPLINES aggregates over 1.5 million cross-sections for 11 key molecular species—including H₂O, CH₄, NH₃, HCN, CO, CO₂, H₂S, CS, CS₂, TiO, and VO—covering wavelengths from 0.3 to 25.0 μm and temperatures ranging from 500 to 2500 K. These data were generated using the line-by-line radiative transfer code, line-by-line RT (libRT). We evaluated the database's impact by comparing synthetic spectra generated with EXOPLINES against those derived from the HITRAN and HITEMP databases. Our analysis indicates that EXOPLINES provides superior accuracy for brown dwarf atmospheres (Teff < 2500 K) and exoplanets with similar temperature profiles, particularly in the near-infrared spectrum (0.3 < λ < 2.5 μm).

This paper examines the theoretical underpinnings of the grounding phase in answer set programming. We establish a one-to-one correspondence between the answer sets of the original program and those resulting from its grounded version, demonstrating that grounding can be interpreted as a specific form of program completion. Furthermore, we show that the process of generating the ground program is equivalent to applying an ultrafilter to the original program's syntax. This perspective yields several new equivalent formulations of grounding and facilitates the extension of the grounding phase to first-order programs.

We establish a comprehensive set of general quantum resource theories (QRTs) defined by freely operable states, offering broad applicability across diverse systems. Within this framework, we derive a first law, formulated as an equation relating free operations to changes in a state's resource value. This theoretical limit is demonstrated to be optimal and universally valid across all QRLs governed by freely operable states. Furthermore, we illustrate the practical significance of this law by deriving specific results for coherence, asymmetry, and thermodynamic resources, while also showing that it addresses and clarifies several open questions in the field.

We examine the relationship between information and statistical moments, establishing that information measures are subject to constraints imposed by various moments. For a class of distributions where the support does not depend on the parameter, we demonstrate that the score function, along with all its derivatives, is bounded within the domain governed by specific moments. This limitation yields inequalities that bound Fisher information against higher-order, complete cumulative cumulants. Additionally, we extend these findings to cases involving unbounded score functions by utilizing stochastic orderings to characterize the dependence between information metrics and higher-order cumulants.

This study examines inference challenges regarding both the mean and covariance in a multivariate time series characterized by a finite number of structural breaks and exhibiting heavy-tailed distributions. We introduce a new multivariate linear model that accommodates these features, including the presence of heavy tails and non-stationarity caused by breaks. We establish results demonstrating that our proposed estimators for mean and covariance achieve optimal rates of convergence despite these difficulties. Furthermore, we verify that our findings hold true even when the exact locations of the breaks are unknown.

We introduce a family of quantum low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes that exhibit simultaneous good performance across encoding, decoding, and error correction capabilities, specifically adhering to the sparsity constraints $O(n)$ for both code rate and degree, while maintaining a distance of at least $\Omega(n)$. Our proposed family features an efficient, sparse generator matrix, enabling rapid encoding operations in $O(n)$ time. Furthermore, we detail a sparse graph representation for the code's parity check matrix that allows for the development of a fault-tolerant, quantum LDPC-based decoder operating in $O(n)$ time. Our construction leverages the graph expansion properties of Cayley graphs derived from groups of order $n$ and dimension $d$, utilizing generators as both connection nodes and edge labels. We demonstrate that an appropriate selection of generators yields a graph with high spectral expansion, leading to the construction of quantum codes with a distance of $\Omega(n)$ and a constant rate. Additionally, we establish that the adjacency matrix of these graphs possesses a spectral gap within a specific region of the complex plane, which is essential for enabling efficient decoding strategies.

This work examines the challenge of finding a distance-$r$ dominating set within a graph $G$ using distributed algorithms. The objective is to identify a subset of vertices such that every node in $G$ is within a distance of $r$ from at least one selected vertex. This problem encompasses several significant cases, including when $r=1$ (standard dominating sets) and when $r=2$ (total dominating sets). We introduce a novel algorithm capable of finding a distance-$r$ dominating set in graphs with a maximum degree of $k$ and a girth of at least $g$ in time proportional to $O(k^2 \log n / (\log k) \cdot \log(g+1))$. This result improves upon the previously best-known complexity bound of $O(k^2 n^{1 - 2/(k^2 - 1)})$ established by Kuhn and Ostlin for this specific parameter range. We further extend our findings to demonstrate that the algorithm remains effective for distance-$r$ domination in graphs that are not sparse, specifically those with a maximum degree of $O(n^{1 - 1/(k^2 - 1)})$.

This study investigates how disorder affects the bulk-boundary correspondence in two-dimensional higher-order topological insulators (HOTIs) based on a square lattice. We analyze a square lattice model where bulk and hinge states are switched by varying either the hopping strength or the on-site potential. Our findings indicate that the correlation between the bulk and edge or hinge properties remains robust against significant disorder. Specifically, in the hinge-terminated scenario, we observe that the hinge states persist despite strong disorder in the bulk. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the number of these surviving hinge states is dictated by the second Chern number.

The CMS collaboration at the CERN Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has recently reported new search results for supersymmetric (SUSY) particles, utilizing proton-proton collision data collected at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV with an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb⁻¹. These searches specifically target scenarios where these particles decay into one or multiple invisible states, a signature consistent with the lightest supersymmetric neutralino acting as a dark matter candidate. The study analyzes final states comprising one or two jets, alongside missing transverse momentum, to constrain various neutralino and chargino models. Key scenarios examined include neutral decays of gluinos and squarks, as well as direct production of the lighter and heavier mass eigenstates of the wino and bino.

We introduce Light Field Neural Rendering (LFNR), a novel framework for novel view synthesis of arbitrary scenes. LFNR achieves this by learning a four-dimensional neural radiance function that represents spatial and color information at any internal point within a scene. To enable rapid and high-quality rendering, our system incorporates a neural Jacobian function designed to compute the derivative of a reference view's ray space relative to a target view. This function allows the algorithm to sample the neural radiance function efficiently, significantly reducing the number of required queries. We demonstrate that our approach excels at rendering both static and dynamic scenes from arbitrary viewpoints and performs robustly even with sparse input data.

Speckle interferometry is a technique that captures high-resolution images of stars by analyzing the interference patterns created within the diffraction limits of a telescope's aperture. This method is highly effective for measuring binary systems, particularly those with components separated by very small angles. We have recently updated our speckle interferometry data from 2020, which was collected using the 4.1-meter Southern Astrophysical Research (SOAR) telescope. We demonstrate that the finite product of chiral algebras defined on the celestial sphere, under a specific condition, possesses a universal central extension whose weights are governed by a quadratic form. This finding provides necessary conditions to determine whether such algebras can be combined via a "fusion" operation to reproduce the interactions of the Standard Model. Furthermore, we show that the tree-level amplitudes of super-Yang-Mills and supergravity in four dimensions adhere to the colour-kinematics duality. This observation leads to the conclusion that the gravitational interaction in supergravity is strictly integrable. Additionally, we establish that the holographic counterpart of the chiral central algebra for a 2D conformal field theory is an integrable quantum spin chain characterized by a non-affine affine Toda algebra as its symmetry structure.

MHD shocks in the solar atmosphere are fundamental to understanding coronal heating and the acceleration of coronal mass ejections. However, pinpointing their exact locations remains difficult because shocks are often obscured by the intense background emission from the surrounding plasma. This study presents the first direct detection of piston-driven shocks in the low corona, achieved through the simultaneous imaging of both the background emission and the shock front itself. We analyzed Extreme ultraviolet Imaging Telescope (EIT) images from the SOHO satellite, which revealed a coronal mass ejection (CME) originating from a pre-existing active region. This event was captured by the Low Frequency Array (LOFAR) at 110 MHz, where the radio data clearly identified a piston shock moving through the quiet Sun corona. By analyzing the spatial relationship between the radio shock and the CME, we determined that the CME propagated at a speed of 120 km/s relative to the shocked plasma. This measurement provides a direct estimate of the post-shock cooling rate, yielding a value of 1.2 x 10^-11 W m^-2. These findings offer valuable insights into the mechanisms governing coronal heating and highlight LOFAR's capability to observe such phenomena directly within the low coronal environment.

We examine the General Two Higgs Doublet Model (GH$\chi$2HM) by incorporating flavour anomalies and the experimental deviation in muon $g-2$ from Standard Model predictions. By performing a comprehensive likelihood analysis, we determine the model's parameter space that aligns with current flavour data, the precise electroweak measurement, and the Higgs boson properties. Our results indicate that the General 2HDM offers a robust explanation for the observed flavour anomalies, with the fit quality improving notably when the $\chi$2HM includes the experimental results for the electroweak sector and the Higgs boson.

This study examines the statistical behavior of 2D superfluid turbulence within the Kraichnov model, characterized by uncorrelated white noise driving, through a novel approach. We derive a functional stochastic differential equation (sDE) on maps defined in both time and space, which governs the stochastic evolution of a piecewise smooth time-continuous, piecewise analytic, yet discontinuous functional map. This map establishes a random, piecewise smooth flow that generates the stochastic vortex configuration and its subsequent dynamics. The derivation leverages the representation of 2D hydrodynamics via a complex potential and utilizes the theory of holomorphic functional differential equations. The resulting functional sDE is shown to possess a unique stationary measure, allowing us to construct a random dynamical system and demonstrate the existence of a random attractor describing the long-term stochastic vortex behavior. Furthermore, we establish that this random attractor corresponds to the random vortex statistics observed in the model. The primary innovation of this method lies in its ability to rigorously analyze the global stochastic dynamics of the system.

We examine the complete state vector of boson sampling for $N$ photons passing through a random $N \times N$ beam splitter setup. Initially, the photons are in unentangled pure states within their respective modes. As the system evolves, the relationship between input and output modes generates particle correlations and entanglement. We analyze the resulting correlations and entanglement properties using the R\'enyi entanglement entropy and von Neumann entropy. Our findings indicate that while correlations increase with the number of photons, the entanglement structure is highly asymmetric: only a few modes become highly entangled, whereas the remainder exhibit significantly lower entanglement levels.

Temporal data analysis is crucial for life science research, where measurements are often recorded over time. However, many existing supervised learning models struggle with the high dimensionality and temporal variability of such data. This study introduces a new network architecture designed to learn short, high-dimensional temporal sequences, featuring a specialized convolutional layer capable of processing high-dimensional inputs. The model was evaluated using two datasets: one comprising molecular dynamics simulations of amyloid-beta fibrils and another consisting of high-dimensional time-series gene expression data from yeast cells. Results demonstrated that the new structure outperformed a standard CNN and a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) in both prediction accuracy and computational efficiency.

Recurrent networks have become a standard component in the deep learning landscape, particularly for tackling tasks that require modeling temporal sequences. This study investigates recurrent networks within the framework of partially observable environments, specifically analyzing their ability to maintain internal representations that enable effective decision-making. We demonstrate that these networks can effectively approximate the optimal belief states required for Markov decision processes, even without explicit reward signals. Furthermore, we illustrate how these learned representations correspond to approximate posterior distributions over latent variables. We also examine the impact of architectural choices and training objectives on the quality of these representations, showing that networks trained with auxiliary tasks can develop more diverse and informative representations. Finally, we explore the utility of these capacity-enhanced representations when used to support the learning of primary, potentially unrewarded objectives.

Action detection involves identifying the start and end times of actions within a video sequence. In a weakly supervised framework, temporal boundaries are not explicitly labeled, yet the entire sequence is tagged with a single class name. This study introduces a graph convolutional network (GCN) to model the temporal evolution of actions. By representing video frames as nodes in a sequence, the method learns the temporal context of actions. The GCN captures spatial relationships between adjacent frames and extends to determine long-term temporal connections, such as the start and end points. Additionally, the model employs a self-attention mechanism to weigh the significance of different frames. Evaluation on the THUMOS14 benchmark demonstrates that the proposed method surpasses current state-of-the-art results.

The Image Similarity Challenge (ISC) 2021 was a multi-task event organized by the Image Analysis and Understanding (IAU) community, designed to evaluate state-of-the-art methods in visual similarity. This study details the evaluation outcomes and key discoveries from the ISC 2021, covering three distinct tasks: the detection of duplicate images, the classification of related images, and the retrieval of visually similar content. The findings indicate that while deep learning models have achieved significant success in duplicate detection and image retrieval, the ranking strategies employed by large-scale systems hold superior potential. Furthermore, advancements in these fields are increasingly driven by self-supervised learning and the integration of textual information.

This research investigates boundary value problems for elliptic and parabolic equations with a highly singular coefficient, defined as $a(x,\varepsilon)=\varepsilon^{-2}(\varepsilon^2+x^2)(\varepsilon^2+(x-x_0)^2)$, where $a_\varepsilon=0$ at exactly two points. The study focuses on the behavior of solutions as $\varepsilon \to 0$, specifically analyzing how these results apply to singular perturbations of classical diffusion models and their associated operators. The analysis yields three distinct applications: solving the singular perturbation of the Sturm-Liouville problem, establishing a quantitative version of large-deviation principles for Brownian motion constrained to the positive half-line, and performing homogenization of operators exhibiting periodic oscillations combined with spatial degeneracy.

This work explores the impact of intense magnetic fields on the properties of nuclear matter, employing the Lorentz-Okubo-Cutkosky (LOKV) method to derive the energy density and pressure. We analyze the behavior of these quantities in both zero and finite volume contexts, specifically investigating the energy density's evolution with varying magnetic field strength. Additionally, we examine how finite volume effects alter the energy density and pressure, contrasting these findings with those from infinite volume calculations.

Federated learning (FL) offers a promising method for training machine learning models while preserving user data privacy. Although differential privacy (DP) is a well-established technique for ensuring privacy in statistical queries, its integration into federated learning remains underutilized. This paper introduces DP-REC, a novel fully private learning framework designed to train a recommendation engine. Our approach combines efficient communication protocols with rigorous differential privacy guarantees. Specifically, we demonstrate that the utility loss incurred by DP-REC is significantly lower than that of existing fully private recommendation systems. Empirical evaluations on real-world datasets confirm that our method achieves superior performance compared to baseline approaches.

The Taurus-Perseus-Auriga molecular cloud complex is recognized as a major site of star formation, hosting numerous young stellar objects (YSOs) and their surrounding disks. This study presents the inaugural detection of Far-UV (FUV) emission from the complex, utilizing data from the GALEX satellite. The FUV spectrum reveals a rich array of emission lines, including atomic hydrogen (H I) and helium (He I), as well as lines from C II, Si II, and Si III ions. These features are analyzed to determine the spatial distribution of interstellar gas and dust, the intensity of the radiation field, and the ionization state of the medium. The analysis indicates that the observed emission lines are primarily generated by the intense radiation fields of YSOs within the complex, with a secondary contribution from diffuse interstellar medium (ISM) components. Furthermore, the findings suggest that the radiation field intensity is significantly higher in the Taurus-Perseus-Auriga complex compared to other well-studied regions like Orion.

Tables are frequently encountered in documents, particularly within PDFs, serving to present data in an organized format. However, the diversity in table designs and document layouts renders the automated extraction of these structures a challenging endeavor. This work introduces a neural network architecture designed to extract tables from source documents. The network leverages state-of-the-art document understanding techniques to generate representations of the visual layout, which are subsequently processed by Graph Neural Networks to identify table cells and their boundaries. The system's performance was evaluated on the Grotab dataset, achieving a F1 score of 84.2%.

This study introduces a multi-stage game framework designed to analyze interactions between a policyholder and an insurance provider characterized by asymmetric information. Specifically, the policyholder holds an unknown risk level unknown relative to the provider, who must decide whether to offer coverage and, if so, set both a premium level and a specific deductible amount. Building on this information gap, the paper investigates how the provider's optimal strategy regarding coverage availability, pricing, and deductible selection depends on the policyholder's risk profile. It further examines the resulting equilibrium strategies for both parties and the subsequent equilibrium outcomes.

This study evaluates the efficacy of using independent population estimation (IPE) techniques to bridge gaps between national censuses, specifically within the context of Mozambique. The research examines three distinct IPE methods: the Area-to-Point Regression Displacement (ATP-Regression) method, the Small-Area Estimation (ATP-Bayesian) method, and the use of remote sensing data to estimate population density. The analysis utilizes census data spanning 1997 to 2017, covering three censuses. The findings indicate that IPE methods are most effective when applied to smaller administrative units, such as wards, rather than larger districts. Furthermore, remote sensing-based density estimation proved to be the most reliable approach for generating high-resolution spatial data. The study concludes that these IPE methods are particularly valuable for generating supplementary estimates between censuses and for monitoring population changes in areas affected by displacement due to conflict or natural disasters.

Approximate Membership Query Filters (AMQF) are probabilistic data structures designed to handle large-scale datasets, offering a space-efficient alternative to Bloom filters by accommodating a configurable false negative rate while maintaining a tunable false positive rate. This research introduces a novel AMQF architecture that eliminates false negatives selectively within a defined subset of the input elements. The structure comprises a standard Bloom filter paired with a specialized data set. The Bloom filter is configured with a lower capacity and a higher estimated false positive rate, whereas the data set is sized to handle a lower, adjustable false positive rate. The system's efficacy is demonstrated through a comparison against the widely used Cuckoo filter. The results indicate that the new AMQF structure requires a smaller total memory footprint and exhibits superior performance in terms of query processing time.

This study explores the mechanism of atom-molecule conversion in ultracold spinor Fermi gases via three-body recombination mediated by a laser. We establish that this process is driven by the coupling of a spin-exchange interaction and an optical dipole-dipole interaction, which together enable the transition between a pair of atoms in opposite spin states and a single molecule in a dipole-bound state. We derive the rate constant for this laser-assisted recombination and analyze its behavior as a function of detuning and polarization. Furthermore, we examine the implications of this process for molecular formation within an ultracold Fermi gas.

We introduce a multi-resolution Smooth Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) framework designed to handle fluid-structure interactions with solid bodies of varying dimensions. This approach employs a specialized boundary treatment that ensures precise alignment between solid boundaries and SPH particles, effectively managing particle penetration and bounce-off phenomena. Additionally, a boundary repositioning technique is utilized to maintain the incompressibility constraint. The validity of this framework is demonstrated through two numerical case studies: a Taylor-Culbick vortex simulation and a wave tank experiment featuring a floating cylinder.

This study introduces a quantum unsupervised learning algorithm for classifying data clusters, which is implemented and tested on a 4-qubit superconducting system. Additionally, the paper proposes a quantum approach to quantum linear discriminant analysis (QLDA), designed to extract meaningful features and enhance data separability. QLAD serves as a foundational component for numerous supervised learning tasks. The utility of this QLDA method is verified through benchmark comparisons against a variety of datasets.

Among the leading TTS models, FastSpeech2 introduced the Pitch Controllable (FC) variant, which allows users to set specific pitch targets for individual phonemes. Building upon this framework, the FastSpeech2-Timbre-Preserving Pitch-Accurate (TPPA) model further enhances pitch controllability through the Pitch-Adaptive Timbre-Preserving Pitch-Accurate (TPPAP) algorithm. This paper introduces a new multi-hop Transformer framework designed for reasoning about tasks involving spatiotemporal dynamics, specifically the 15-Way Object (STO) problem. The proposed model features a novel multi-modal architecture that handles both natural language inputs and visual inputs, which consist of a sequence of images depicting an object's state changes. The framework's core innovation lies in a new multi-modal attention mechanism that enables the integration of linguistic and visual information to perform sequential reasoning. The model is evaluated on the 15-Way STO benchmark, demonstrating performance that surpasses current state-of-the-art approaches. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/ashishku/MH-HOPPER.

This study examines lepton-pair production alongside a bottom quark-antiquark pair at the LHC, focusing on the differential cross-sections for transverse momenta and the invariant mass of the lepton pair. These analyses are based on a dataset of 139 fb$^{-1}$ collected at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV by the CMS experiment. Results are compared with predictions from Monte Carlo simulations that incorporate various parton distribution function models. Furthermore, a fit to the lepton-pair transverse mass distribution yields a $W$ boson mass measurement of $m_W = 80.426 \pm 0.035 \text{(stat)} \pm 0.029 \text{(syst)}$ GeV.

Telepresence robots offer a remote means of social engagement and have become a popular method for enhancing virtual interaction experiences. However, current remote control mechanisms often fail to adequately address user QoE. This study introduces a novel interactive QoE evaluation framework for telepresence, where users independently adjust the virtual avatar's presence within the virtual environment to mirror their real-world physical location. The research examines how this avatar positioning influences the interactive QoE of remote operators, specifically focusing on the distinct effects of latency and bandwidth constraints. The findings indicate that latency exerts a more significant negative impact on QoE than limited bandwidth, and this effect intensifies as the user's physical distance from the robot increases. Consequently, this work underscores the critical necessity of incorporating interactive QoE metrics into the design and optimization of future telepresence systems.

This guide offers a straightforward introduction to Bayesian hierarchical linear regression, covering both conceptual foundations and practical implementation. It begins by outlining the key distinctions between Bayesian and frequentist approaches, followed by an exploration of how hierarchical structures differ from standard linear regression. Additionally, it details the specific advantages of hierarchical models, particularly in handling sparse data. The text further clarifies the role of prior distributions, examining both their theoretical importance and their impact on model outcomes. Finally, it provides examples of prior selection strategies and concludes with a practical demonstration of the entire workflow using the `rstan` package in R.

"Mafia" (alternatively known as "Werewolf") is a popular social deduction game where players, divided into opposing teams, aim to eliminate the rival group through strategic voting. In the "Mafia" variant, a non-communicating mafia group with a limited size seeks to outlast a defenseless group of civilians. This paper presents a mathematical model of the game dynamics, utilizing a discrete-time, continuous-state framework. This approach represents the population counts for both roles as continuous variables and derives a system of ordinary differential equations to model their evolution. This mathematical formulation enables the characterization of the probable outcome, determining whether the mafia or civilians ultimately prevail. This work serves as a foundational reference for analyzing the game's behavior and for subsequent modeling of its stochastic variations.

This study investigates the simultaneous growth of two giant planets within a protoplanetary disk, aiming to determine if this mechanism can explain the existence of super-Jovian masses. We utilize a 2D hydrodynamic code to simulate disk evolution and planet growth, incorporating a gas accretion model that accounts for the cooling of the planetary envelope. Our results indicate that while simultaneous accretion does not significantly alter the final masses of the planets compared to isolated scenarios, it substantially affects the disk's evolution. Specifically, the presence of a second planet reduces the rate of gas consumption, thereby extending the lifetime of the protoplanetary disk. We also examine the dynamical interactions between the growing bodies and their impact on the system, concluding that concurrent growth serves as a crucial factor in modeling the co-evolution of planet formation and disk dissipation.

Carbon nanotubes (CNTs) are highly promising for both nanoelectronics and energy-storage applications, yet a major hurdle remains: distinguishing intrinsic electronic behavior from extraneous effects caused by phonons and defects. This study presents the first experimental observation of phonon-mediated transport in an ensemble of armchair carbon nanotubes, utilizing a single metallic armchair nanotube (diameter ~1.2 nm) suspended between gold electrodes. At low temperatures, a pronounced nonlinearity emerges in the current-voltage characteristics, which is attributed to phonon-assisted tunneling. This phenomenon is confirmed by comparing experimental data with a tight-binding model that incorporates phonon assistance. Furthermore, the research indicates that phonon-driven transport in armchair nanotube ensembles occurs at a lower threshold phonon energy than previously recorded in zigzag nanotubes.

Clustering is a fundamental technique in unsupervised learning, widely used to identify patterns within unlabeled datasets. However, traditional clustering methods face significant limitations when applied to high-dimensional data, primarily due to the "curse of dimensionality," which causes a degradation in performance. This paper introduces a novel feature-weighted fuzzy k-means (FWK) clustering approach designed specifically to enhance effectiveness in high-dimensional environments. The proposed method assigns individual weights to feature variables to facilitate more precise cluster formation. The weighting mechanism is grounded in an entropy-based metric that evaluates the distinctiveness of each feature. The validity of this approach was verified through experiments on both low- and high-dimensional data sets, with results demonstrating that the algorithm achieves superior performance compared to existing methods across various evaluation metrics.

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have become a cornerstone in machine learning, particularly for handling large-scale deep learning tasks. Although the literature contains various algorithms for training MoE architectures, a critical flaw remains: these methods are not guaranteed to converge to population-level optima. This issue is especially problematic when determining convergence points, as suboptimal selections can severely undermine model performance. Addressing this gap, this work introduces the first algorithms proven to achieve population-level optimality. Specifically, we formulate MoE structures as non-convex optimization challenges and prove that, under mild conditions, both our proposed methods and their convergence behavior align with population-level objectives. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that the number of samples required for convergence scales polynomially with the model's dimensionality. Furthermore, we show that our approach extends to broader classes of non-convex problems, including but not limited to deep neural networks.

This paper investigates chip-firing games defined on directed graphs lacking an Euler characteristic, with a particular focus on their Jacobian's relationship to a specific Prym variety. The discussion begins by examining the natural map from a specific linear equivalence class space to this Prym variety, demonstrating its surjectivity under stated conditions. Furthermore, we establish a dimension for this surjective map's kernel, offering a combinatorial interpretation for what we term the "reduced critical graph." Finally, drawing inspiration from Baker's theorem in algebraic geometry, we utilize this kernel to construct a non-trivial linear equivalence involving a specific divisors and an effective divisor determined by graph topology.

We investigate how cosmic birefringence serves as a probe for global internal symmetries within quantum gravity models, which are theoretically expected to be spontaneously broken. This phenomenon, characterized by a global rotation of linearly polarized light, can be detected through a comparison of Planck's B-mode polarization data with lower-ℓ data from SPT-3G. Our analysis reveals that such a rotation angle is constrained to be less than 0.34 radians at 95% confidence, a limit that effectively rules out many global symmetries found in specific quantum gravity frameworks. We also assess the impact of theoretical uncertainties regarding the associated effective couplings and find that the current constraints remain robust.

The UV-optical photometry of the globular cluster NGC 4147 was conducted using observations from the AstroSat satellite, specifically from the Ultraviolet Imaging Telescope (UVIT) and Optical Telescope Array (OTAs). These data were supplemented by UVIT photometry from the cluster NGC 6397. The study involved the analysis of 1,000 stars in NGC 4147 and 1,000 stars in NGC 6397, with a focus on identifying UV bright stars (UBSs) defined by an excess in the $U_{255}$ band relative to the $B_{444}$ band. The derived parameters for NGC 4147 include a distance modulus of $(m-M)_0 = 13.41 \pm 0.05$ mag, a metallicity of $[\text{Fe}/\text{H}] = -1.71 \pm 0.10$ dex, and an estimated age of 11.9 Gyr. The globular cluster's line-of-sight velocity was measured as $-101.1 \pm 1.1$ km s$^{-1}$. The authors demonstrate that the $b$-principle is satisfied for every surjective homomorphism $\rho: \pi_n(G) \to \pi_{n+1}(G)$ where the group $G$ is an $n$-connected topological group and the dimension $n$ is at least 3. This finding establishes that the Mumford conjecture holds for every Eilenberg-MacLane space $K(\mathbb Z, n)$ within the range $n \geq 3$.

Transferability serves as a critical factor in enhancing generalization within deep learning, yet the community has reached conflicting conclusions regarding its source. Some researchers attribute superior performance primarily to the source domain, whereas others emphasize the role of the target domain. This study addresses these discrepancies by examining two fundamental aspects of transferability: the source and the target. By utilizing a newly developed transferability benchmark, we demonstrate that transferability significantly boosts performance in both domains, challenging previous perspectives. Furthermore, we identify a key limitation in existing evaluation methods: they fail to detect transferability gains in cases where the final model underperforms compared to a non-transported baseline. This flaw leads to the erroneous conclusion that transferability is ineffective in such scenarios.

We investigate how network structure influences the spread of information, specifically examining the relationship between diffusion speed and network modularity. Our findings indicate that information travels significantly faster in modular networks compared to those with uniform structures, a result we attribute to the presence of community boundaries. These barriers create chokepoints that concentrate traffic, accelerating propagation. Our research further shows that this mechanism holds true regardless of whether diffusion is modeled as a deterministic process or a stochastic one, and regardless of the specific model parameters used. We also explore how varying the strength of these barriers affects propagation dynamics. Our analytical methods are versatile and can be adapted to numerous other diffusion models.

The FLRW metric is a solution to the Einstein's equations and describes a universe that expands or contracts uniformly in all directions. It is characterized by the scale factor a(t) and curvature parameter k, which can take values of -1, 0, or +1. The metric takes the following form:

ds² = -dt² + a²(t) [ dr² / (1-k r²) + r² (dθ² + sin²θ dφ²) ]

where (t, r, θ, φ) are comoving coordinates. The scale factor a(t) is determined by the Friedmann equations, which relate the expansion rate to the energy density and pressure of the universe's contents.

Observations indicate that our universe is spatially flat (k=0) and expanding at an accelerating rate. In this context, the scale factor follows a power law a(t) ∝ t^(2/3) for a matter-dominated universe or a(t) ∝ e^(Ht) for a cosmological constant-dominated universe, where H is the Hubble constant.

The numerical evaluation of a unamplified discrete-time channel model is examined. A regular perturbation approach yields a representation of the nonlinear input-output relationship as a set of weighted terms, where coefficients depend on the nonlinearity parameter and powers of the input signal. Power-series expansion is utilized to determine these coefficients. Discrete-time accuracy is analyzed by applying a series of approximations, including the power-series truncation, to the set of governing equation parameters.

Mobile devices are increasingly central to modern life, serving as primary gateways to online platforms and essential services. This paper examines security vulnerabilities within the Android operating system, specifically focusing on evasion attacks that exploit problem-space manipulation. These attacks deceive existing security mechanisms by altering the input space of applications, thereby bypassing detection. We analyze the evolution of these threats, outlining their historical development and categorizing them into three main types: input space, output space, and model space evasion. Additionally, the survey explores the defensive countermeasures used to detect and mitigate these attacks, identifies current research challenges, and proposes directions for future work.

Orchestration platforms are essential for deploying and managing applications across vast distributed systems. While numerous such platforms exist, each typically relies on a specific, often rigid container model that constrains application development by limiting the available programming languages and runtime environments. To address these constraints, we introduce Ozy, a generalized orchestration container designed to support the full spectrum of language and environment combinations. We detail the architectural structure of the Ozy container, its integration with the Ozy orchestration framework, and the corresponding system implementation. Furthermore, we present empirical findings from both performance benchmarks and a comprehensive study of a real-world deployment.

The recent discovery of binary black hole mergers by the LIGO-Virgo collaboration has reignited interest in primordial black holes (PBHs) as a cosmological dark matter candidate. Specifically, constraints regarding dark matter abundance have been established for BH masses exceeding $10^2 M_\odot$. This study examines a specific scenario where isolated black holes with masses greater than $10^2 M_\odot$ serve as dark matter candidates, described by the Thakurta metric. We demonstrate that this particular solution is incompatible with the no-hair theorem, rendering it physically invalid. Consequently, findings from [arXiv:1905.02921]—which analyzed LIGO-Virgo constraints on cosmological black holes using the Thakurta metric—remain unaffected, as our results align with those conclusions.

Planet formation via pebble accretion is heavily influenced by the local environment, particularly the location of the water snowline. This study examines how local density perturbations in the dust disk impact the accumulation rate of pebbles by planets. Our findings indicate that in an undisturbed disk, planetesimals can form within approximately 100,000 years, whereas local density enhancements accelerate this process to as little as 10,000 years. Conversely, the presence of a gas giant migrating inward creates a dust trap that significantly boosts pebble accretion rates. These results demonstrate that local variations in dust density play a crucial role in the formation of planetesimals and the subsequent accretion of pebbles.

Overparameterized models have gained significant traction in machine learning due to their superior generalization capabilities, yet the specific conditions under which they outperform their parameterized counterparts remain unclear. This paper introduces a novel framework for overparameterized models that attributes these performance gains to restricted computational constraints. We demonstrate that, under certain assumptions, optimizing a minimum-complexity function yields the same results as an overparameterized approach. Furthermore, we establish that when the optimal solution of this constrained optimization problem lies within a specific manifold, overparameterization leads to improved model performance.

The primary objective is to demonstrate that the Ruzsa covering lemma can be enhanced by substituting Bohr sets in place of ordinary covering sets. To achieve this, we establish that the Ruzsa product of two sets with positive measure (or finite measure, as appropriate) contains a Bohr set with the density at least as large as the product of the sets' measures. We further show that the parameters of this resulting Bohr set can be explicitly defined as functions of the parameters of the input sets and their associated Bohr sets.

We also prove that the sum of two sets with positive measure contains a Bohr set with the density at least as large as the product of the sets' densities. We show that the parameters of this resulting Bohr set can be explicitly defined as functions of the parameters of the sets involved.
