This paper introduces a mathematical model and a branch-and-cut algorithm to address the urban dial-a-ride problem. In this context, a fleet of vehicles must collect passengers from designated pick-up points and transport them to their corresponding drop-off points. The objective is to determine the number of vehicles required and plan their routes to minimize total cost while adhering to specific constraints. This study focuses on a problem variant that permits multiple pick-up and drop-off stops per trip, incorporates time windows for all stops, and accounts for passenger transfer times and detours. We propose a new polyhedral study that yields a polytope definition for a relaxed version of the problem. Leveraging this formulation, we construct a branch-and-cut solver that utilizes cutting planes to separate the resulting polyhedral inequalities. Computational experiments demonstrate that the algorithm produces high-quality solutions for instances involving up to 100 pick-up and drop-off points.

We introduce MM-KP, a new multi-modal pretraining framework tailored for e-commerce tasks. Unlike existing approaches, our model explicitly integrates knowledge of various modalities to facilitate more effective representation learning. We achieve this by leveraging a Knowledge Graph representing relationships among entities and attributes within e-commerce, alongside a multi-modal transformer designed to process both image and text data. We evaluate the model using a pretrain-and-fine-tune strategy on e-commerce specific tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques in multi-modal e-commerce pretraining.

Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a prevalent and fatal neurodegenerative condition that typically begins with a mild decline in cognitive function before progressing to severe dementia. Currently, there is no cure for AD, and existing treatments only temporarily alleviate symptoms. Consequently, there is an urgent need for advanced diagnostic and prognostic tools to enable earlier detection and more precise prediction of disease trajectory. This study introduces a novel deep learning architecture designed to analyze longitudinal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data for estimating the likelihood of AD progression. The model utilizes a specialized Deep InfoMax framework, which employs a dedicated encoder-decoder pair for each time point within a patient's scan series. These encoders generate condition vectors representing the AD state at each stage, which are then fed into a decoder to reconstruct the original MRI. Experimental results indicate that the proposed Deep InfoMax approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methodologies in predicting disease progression.

The architecture's core component, a grammality-based recurrent neural network, utilizes the principles of context-free grammar to drive sequential information processing. The interaction-based recurrent neural network, designed to capture context-sensitive structures, facilitates data exchange between the two sub-networks. The core innovation lies in this inter-network interaction, which enhances the model's capacity for comprehensive language semantics interpretation. We introduce a theoretical framework describing a correlated metal exhibiting strong spin-orbit coupling, where electron-electron interactions are mediated not only by electric charge but also by spin. This mechanism, occurring in the presence of robust magnetism, has been demonstrated within a quantum circuit simulator, revealing a distinct difference in the nature of spin and charge excitations. These findings are expected to apply to materials such as oxides and heavy metals, where spin-dependent interactions play a significant role.

We propose a new framework for particle dark matter that relies on the concept of metastability. In this model, the stable particle that constitutes the dark matter is a bound state of lighter particles, which annihilate into standard model particles. In order to achieve the correct relic density, these stable composite particles must have an effective annihilation cross section that is significantly larger than the thermal average. We demonstrate that this can be accomplished if the initial ground state of the system transitions to the actual stable fermionic bound state. We apply this mechanism to the case of a pseudoscalar dark matter candidate, the axion, and find that it can account for the observed relic abundance. Furthermore, we explore the possibility of producing these states in high-energy proton-proton collisions, such as those at the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC).

The regulatory bodies, such as the FDA, have recently granted approval for numerous AI-driven software as medical devices (SaMD) designed to detect and diagnose diseases. Despite this approval, these models often exhibit reduced accuracy when deployed in environments that differ from their training data distributions. Addressing this challenge, this paper introduces a method to estimate a predictive model's performance when training and testing data follow distinct distributions. Our approach utilizes a subset of data comprising both training samples and new, unlabeled test instances to construct a nonparametrically derived, valid, and distribution-agnostic confidence interval for the failure rate. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this methodology through applications to medical image classification and electronic health record (EHR) analysis.

We introduce a novel biasing methodology for molecular dynamics simulations that leverages the DNA base pairs' intrinsic tendency to remain flat. By applying biasing potentials to enforce planarity, we significantly expand the exploration of DNA's conformational landscape. This approach proves highly effective in various simulations, including those designed to populate rare states, facilitate melting processes, and model transitions between B-DNA and Z-DNA. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this strategy is broadly applicable to other biological systems, offering substantial benefits for the general enhanced sampling of biomolecular structures.

The Arithmetic Encoding (ANS) serves as a highly efficient entropy coder that has been widely adopted in various standards. This paper analyzes the theoretical underpinnings of ANS, specifically the bit replenishment process, and establishes a general theorem that includes recent ANS variants as special cases. Furthermore, we introduce a modified replenishment scheme designed to enhance the coder's throughput.

The dielectric constant of the pore solution within cement-based materials is derived from the molar concentrations of their ionic components. Consequently, the total dielectric permittivity in these materials represents a composite of contributions from the pore solution, the solid cement paste phase, and the entrained air. These derived equations facilitate the modeling of dielectric behavior in cement-based substances across a broad range of frequencies and the entire dielectric spectrum.

This article provides an overview of experimental findings and theoretical progress regarding heavy-heavy hadronic molecules, with a specific emphasis on tetramolecules composed of two heavy meson-antimeson pairs. It begins by examining the experimental techniques used to identify exotic hadrons, followed by a detailed discussion on the theoretical frameworks describing heavy-heavy molecular formations. Furthermore, the work analyzes potential XZI molecular structures, explores the search for di-XZI molecular candidates within the LHCb data, and outlines future research directions.

This paper examines the driving forces behind the advancement of swarms of military drones. To achieve this, we utilize Natural Language Processing techniques to analyze English-language research publications concerning swarm drones. Specifically, we extract features such as mission objectives, driving factors, challenges, and hardware or software components. Additionally, we assess how these attributes have evolved over time, noting that the methodology can be generalized to other areas of research.

We introduce a method for deriving cosmological parameters from the three-point correlation function of the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest, specifically examining the quadrupole of the Q-function. This approach yields a 3$\sigma$ constraint on the matter fluctuation amplitude, $f\sigma_8$, reaching $0.104 \pm 0.026$ based on 2000 hydrodynamic simulations from the IllustrisTorch project. These simulations were generated using the 2015 Planck cosmology at a resolution of $128^3$ $h^{-1}$ Mpc. Our technique offers a significant advantage by circumventing the need to model the complex, non-linear evolution of the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest, which is typically a major source of systematic uncertainty. We validate our results by contrasting them with the Lyman-$\alpha$ quadrupole of the BAO correlation function; despite the limited volume of our simulations, our derived $f\sigma_8$ limits are competitive with those obtained from large-scale BAO analyses.

This study presents the first experimental results on swapping longitudinal and transverse emittances, achieved using a solenoidal device engineered to maximize the exchange of longitudinal and lateral beam properties. The apparatus, designed to facilitate precise manipulation of these emittances while ensuring their conservation, was tested using the proton beam at INFN-LNS. Initial measurements confirm the successful transfer of transverse emittance into the longitudinal domain, with a significant reduction in beam energy spread. Furthermore, the experiment validates the reversible nature of this process by demonstrating the complete return of the transverse energy distribution to the longitudinal plane.

Pedestrian navigation in urban settings is heavily influenced by social interactions, yet current pedestrian trajectory prediction models often neglect these dynamics. This paper introduces a sliding sequential conditional variational autoencoder (ssCVAE) designed to forecast multi-pedestrian paths while integrating socially aware information. The model utilizes a socially aware recurrent neural network (SA-RNN) to extract interpersonal interactions from historical data, which are then combined with the current state to compute the next trajectory. The proposed ssCVAE leverages a flexible sliding window mechanism to generate multiple potential future paths and employs a mixture of Gaussians within a variational framework to refine latent variable estimation. This approach enhances the accuracy of both peak velocity and path length predictions. Empirical evaluations on the Princeton University Pedestrian Dataset (Princeton Ped1) and the Georgia Tech Pedestrian Dataset (GTzed) demonstrate that the socially aware sa-RNN-enhanced ssCVAE surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods.

This study investigates the complexity of two distinct Boltzmann machine architectures: the restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM) and the deep Boltzmann machine (DBM). We demonstrate that the Lyapunov function of a Boltzmann machine can be interpreted as a measure of its complexity. Furthermore, we establish that the average Lyapunov function serves as an effective predictor for the mean energy of the system's steady state. Additionally, our analysis reveals that this average Lyapunov function scales linearly with the number of units in the network.

The results indicate that RBMs possess lower complexity compared to DBMs, a trend that intensifies as network size increases. We also observe a direct link between Lyapunov function values and the mean energy of the resulting steady state.

Decentralized algorithms facilitate Human-Swarm Interactions (HSI) by enabling direct communication between users and individual swarm agents without centralized mediation. This study introduces a method for identifying hand gestures to interpret user inputs, utilizing a decentralized approach for this specific task. Additionally, the validity of this method is confirmed through experiments conducted on the decentralized Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) environment known as "Swarm Learning."

This study evaluates a multi-model architecture designed to enhance the classification of blood cells. The research compares two distinct neural network types: one based on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and the other on Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN). The CNN component extracts spatial features from the input images, while the RNN captures temporal dynamics from the sequence of features identified by the CNN. The combined output of these integrated models is then compared against the performance of each individual model in isolation. The findings indicate that the hybrid approach surpasses standalone models, yielding higher accuracy in detecting various types of blood cells.

We introduce a novel, numerically efficient variational counterdiabatic (CD) driving protocol designed for ground-state preparation within the one-dimensional Hubbard model. By deriving the exact ground states of the model's nearest-neighbor projected Anderson-Hubbard dimer as variational states, we construct an efficient approximator for the adiabaticity-bypassing CD Hamiltonian. Our results demonstrate that this variational scheme significantly reduces both the computational demands and optical forces compared to other continuous driver strategies. Furthermore, we evaluate the scheme's performance on larger single-occupancy systems, revealing that it scales linearly with respect to both the required time step and the state of excitation.

This research introduces a rapid decolorization technique that leverages a novel color temperature metric. The proposed decolorization process is derived from an empirical formula, which demonstrates performance comparable to methods based on the physical definition of color temperature. The algorithm's efficiency allows for high-speed operation, rendering it ideal for real-time tone mapping applications. The document details the color temperature model, the specific formulation for calculating temperature from chromaticity coordinates, and the implementation of the rapid decolorization method. The model's validity is confirmed through extensive testing and comparisons with other established approaches. The study concludes by highlighting the significant potential of the color temperature model in advancing the field of tone mapping.

Let $(S, d)$ be a surface equipped with a metric that is non-positively curved under the definition of the Cheeger-Gromoll. If $X$ is a topological branched covering mapping onto $S$ with a finite set of branch points, and $m$ represents the local degree of $f$ at $x$, then the following inequality holds: $\rho_x \leq m\pi/2$. Here, $\rho_x$ is the angle of the branch point at $x$, and $m$ is the local degree of $f$ at $x$. We also provide examples to show that the constant $\pi/2$ in the inequality cannot be replaced by a larger value.

We introduce a novel laser-plasma accelerator designed to generate high-field regions within a laser-driven plasma channel surrounding an independent plasma wakefield. This configuration facilitates the acceleration of electrons via the combined action of a plasma mirror and the bow shock created by the pump laser, resulting in exceptionally steep mirrors that support strong electromagnetic fields. This architecture offers a streamlined approach to achieving the photon-photon interactions necessary for non-linear quantum electrodynamics.

This work examines the sensitivity of the 13 TeV LHC to the soft-breaking $Z_2$ parameter, $m_{12}$, within a Type-II Two-Higgs-Doublet Model (2HDM). We analyze how this parameter influences the sensitivity to the lighter CP-even Higgs boson, $h$, and the heavy vector-like bosons ($H$ and $A$), utilizing the Higgs Signal Strength ($\mu$) and the $\kappa$ framework. Our findings indicate that the $m_{12}$ influence on $h$ signal strength remains largely independent of its sign, whereas the effect on the heavy bosons, $H$ and $A$, is sign-dependent. We further determine the exclusion limits for $m_{12}$ across various sign configurations and compare these results with those derived from LEP, the Higgs mechanism, and electroweak precision data.

The study analyzes consistency issues, result existence, and result enumeration within this context. The authors present a finite model order, union-free first-order theory that is decidable, and provide a polynomial time algorithm to determine consistency. This article introduces pyStoNED, a Python library designed for nonparametric linear envelope (NED) regression and the estimation of production frontiers. As an extension of the original StoNE algorithm by Armstron, Armstron, and Armstron (StoNE: StoNE, StoNE, StoNE), which was previously implemented in R via the dedicated R package, pyStoNEM translates these capabilities to Python. The authors highlight the utility of pyStoNEM in facilitating cross-language comparison of results and code structures. Furthermore, the text outlines the software's internal architecture and provides a comprehensive example illustrating its application to linear envelope regression tasks.

We introduce a method for detecting the light Higgs boson within the $t \bar t \phi$ channel at the LHC, focusing on the scenario where the Higgs boson decays into a pair of bottom quarks. This analysis leverages the substantial top quark mass to enhance the signal-to-background ratio. We evaluate the method's sensitivity using the 139 fb$^{-1}$ of data collected at the LHC, covering the full CMS detector acceptance. Our results indicate that the current method can probe a Higgs boson mass up to 120 GeV with a sensitivity of 120 fb, which is slightly less than the projected sensitivity of ATLAS and CMS for the same region. We also discuss the potential for future improvements in this method.

Pre-trained language models (PLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in semantic parsing, achieving state-of-the-word results even on datasets with scarce annotations. Despite this, current state-of-the-art approaches typically rely on supervised fine-tuning, which demands extensive labeled data. This paper introduces Unsupervised and Few-Shot Parsing (UP), a novel framework that leverages PLMs to conduct semantic parsing without any annotated examples. By utilizing PLMs' inherent ability to extract entities and relationships from vast corpora, UP refines these predictions through an unsupervised, self-supervised process. The method employs a two-stage strategy: initially, it performs semantic role labeling (SRL) by aligning verb-centered context windows with existing SRL taxonomies; subsequently, it generates logical forms by mapping these role labels to the logic layer. Empirical results across multiple datasets reveal that UP achieves significant performance improvements over prior state-of-the-art methods, delivering an average relative gain of 10.5% in execution accuracy and 11.3% in F1 scores.

This study introduces a KDD Open Source Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) toolkit designed to recognize German. We detail the synthesis of a German speech corpus by merging two existing datasets and present performance metrics from our German language model. The results indicate that our system achieves a Word Error Rate (WER) of 22.2% on the TIGER dataset and a lower WER of 16.1% on the TIGER dataset. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of 30 candidate Be-type stars within the 30 Doradus (N36) nebula, utilizing multi-epoch optical photometry and spectroscopy. The sample consists of 23 objects with existing spectra and 31 with new spectra obtained. Based on the photometric data, we identified 11 stars exhibiting Be characteristics, 10 showing probable Be features, and 9 classified as non-Be. Spectroscopic examination of the 30 newly observed targets revealed 11 with distinct emission lines and 19 without. These objects are categorized as Be, Bp, and non-Be stars, with the latter two groups comprising 11 and 19 stars, respectively. Be stars are defined by their emission lines, while Bp stars are characterized by line profiles resembling those of main-sequence B stars but with line widths similar to Be stars. The spectral properties of the Bp stars align with those of the Be stars, suggesting they are likely in a pre-Be evolutionary phase. Furthermore, we identified 11 stars with emission lines that lack the typical Be star classification; these are termed "emission line non-Be stars" (ELnonBes). These ELnonBes differ from Be stars in their emission line profiles, which are narrower and exhibit a higher equivalent width of the H$\alpha$ line.

Inverse Text Normalization (IT) converts written text from spoken forms into standardized numerical or symbolic representations. While data-driven models have achieved success in this area, performance often lags on datasets with infrequent entities, such as dates, due to insufficient training examples. This study investigates data augmentation as a means to enhance the training data for these rare categories. We assess three augmentation techniques: Random Forest, Randomly Generated, and Randomly Created. Our findings indicate that our proposed Randomly Created approach yields the best results, surpassing a random baseline by 0.2 F1 score and a Randomly Generated method by 0.1 F1. Furthermore, we demonstrate that leveraging an IT model pre-trained on one domain can boost the effectiveness of these augmentation strategies.

This paper establishes a Faber-Krahn inequality concerning the principal eigenvalue of the Hermitian operator under Robin boundary conditions on a bounded region of $\mathbb{R}^n$; it further derives this result via monotonicity arguments related to the Robin parameter.

This paper introduces a new kernel method that transforms input data into non-fungible kernel (NFT-K) representations, where each data point receives an individualized kernel function rather than a uniform one. By integrating concepts from graph learning and attention mechanisms, the method constructs a dynamic kernel for every sample based on its contextual relationships with others within the dataset. We provide theoretical justification for the approach and demonstrate its application in two distinct areas: learning on manifolds and graph classification. Empirical results confirm that the NFT-K method achieves superior performance compared to traditional kernel techniques in both graph classification benchmarks and tasks involving ribosome profiling data on manifolds.

Non-Hermitian systems exhibit unique topological classifications, including point-gap topology. While correlations are generally thought to destroy this classification, we demonstrate that one-dimensional non-interacting systems with point-gap topology retain it despite the introduction of interactions. Furthermore, we identify a non-trivial topological phase in a interacting variant of the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model that features chiral symmetry but lacks particle-hole symmetry. Our findings indicate that the reduction of the point gap by interactions is mitigated when chiral symmetry is maintained, allowing for a new topological order. This behavior is consistent with the classification of free-fermion systems with chiral symmetry, which permits stable point-gap topology in the presence of correlations.

This study examines the inclusion of social characteristics—such as age, gender, and emotion—in synthetic speech. We evaluate existing approaches for feature extraction and propose new methodologies, specifically targeting age synthesis. Our analysis reveals that current techniques for creating aged speech suffer from artifacts and lack robustness, prompting the introduction of a novel, robust age synthesis algorithm. Additionally, we present a new deep learning-based method for generating aged speech that demonstrates superior performance over existing models.

We introduce a novel light dark matter framework featuring a dark sector characterized by $U(1)_D$ gauge symmetry and dark-charged fermions. The dark photon acquires mass via symmetry breaking driven by a complex scalar doublet, while dark fermions gain their masses through interactions with tetraquarks composed of four quarks in a color-singlet state. This specific quark composition ensures the requisite dark fermion charge assignments for compatibility with current experimental constraints. The model's symmetries, including $U(1)_{B-L}$ and a discrete $A_4$ group, enable the radiative generation of neutrino masses, yielding predictions that align with observed oscillation data. Additionally, the framework predicts several new particles and associated phenomena at the LHC, offering distinct avenues for future verification.

This study investigates triaxial nuclei within the framework of the minimal length concept, applying it to the three-dimensional Bohr-Mottelson model. We derive the corresponding Hamiltonian and employ a generalized Hill-Wheeler potential to calculate eigenenergies and wave functions. Results indicate that incorporating the minimal length concept significantly impacts collective rotational bands. Furthermore, we compute energy levels and wave functions for the triaxial nuclei $^{152}$Gd and $^{152}$Er, comparing our findings with experimental data.

Recently, multiple studies have focused on Golay Complementary Arrays (GCAs) due to their capacity to produce Golay Complementary Arrays (GCDS) with larger coherent processing gains in GCD S applications. This paper introduces new construction methods for polyphase GCAs, which can be utilized to build polyphase Golay Complementary Difference Sets (pGCDS). Specifically, our approaches include a generalized version of the Discrete Pseudo-Random Sequence (DPRS) method, a revised approach inspired by Reeds, a method by Lin and Yang, two distinct variants of a Beutler approach, and an original method developed by the authors. These proposed techniques offer a means to construct specific configurations of these arrays effectively.

Detecting changes in remote sensing imagery is crucial for monitoring environmental shifts, yet it remains a difficult task, particularly for high-dimensional hyperspectral data where the count of spectral bands creates significant challenges. This paper introduces an unsupervised deep learning-based change detection framework that operates without manual annotations. The method employs two convolutional autoencoders to extract hierarchical features, which are then combined through feature fusion to identify alterations. The fusion mechanism integrates both the summed and difference outputs of the aligned features to pinpoint modifications. The approach's efficacy is validated using two benchmark datasets: the Indian Pines and the Conifer Forests scenes.

This study examines the relationship between residual entropy and viscosity in molecular fluids and potential models. We utilize residual entropy to quantify the gap between actual fluid entropy and an ideal gas state, demonstrating that this metric captures the essential physics governing viscosity. Specifically, we find that reduced (dimensionless) viscosity correlates with residual entropy through a simple exponential function. This exponential link holds true for a broad spectrum of molecular fluids and various potential models, including those representing water. Furthermore, we establish that reduced viscosity is inversely proportional to residual entropy via this exponential mechanism. Consequently, we conclude that reduced viscosity is exponentially tied to residual entropy across diverse molecular fluids and potential models, including water models. This relationship highlights the critical role of residual entropy in determining viscosity, showing that it varies inversely with an exponential dependence.

This study explores a novel $\Lambda$CDM cosmological model characterized by a periodic scale factor, $a(t)$, which is a necessary component for accommodating a matter-dominated epoch. While this model is not viable at extreme temporal scales ($t \to \infty$ or $t \to -\infty$), it accurately reproduces the transition between radiation and matter domination at intermediate times. By employing a Bayesian framework, the researchers constrained the key parameters of this model using combined datasets from Planck, BICEP2, and the SDSS. The resulting confidence intervals for the Hubble constant, $H_0$, are $67.1^{+1.1}_{-1.2}$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$ for the periodic case and $67.1^{+1.1}_{-1.2}$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$ for the single-period variant, both of which align closely with the standard cosmological framework.

The Invariant-set theory, a superdeterministic hidden-variable model, posits that certain dynamical systems evolve along specific solution paths within a high-dimensional state space known as invariant sets. This theory offers an explanation for quantum correlations by suggesting these paths encode hidden variables. A central tenet of superdeterminism is the rejection of measurement independence, implying that hidden variables may correlate with experimental settings. This framework also provides an alternative to the standard assumption of an infinite ensemble in statistical mechanics, allowing for the use of finite ensembles. Furthermore, superdeterministic models can be tested by examining the statistical distribution of latent variables or their associated phases. Specifically, testing the Invariant-set theory involves analyzing the phase distributions of a two-particle system; if the theory holds, these phases should follow a uniform distribution. However, numerical simulations of the Double-slit experiment using Invariant-set dynamics reveal a non-uniform distribution of two-particle phases. Consequently, the Invariant-set theory fails the test of statistical distribution for hidden-variable phases in a double-slit context, indicating it is not empirically viable.

This paper introduces a keyword spotting architecture designed for IoT devices, leveraging a recurrent network with attention mechanisms and a classifier, all trained using a single dataset. The study evaluates the impact of different data augmentation techniques and analyzes how varying amounts of training data influence model performance. The results indicate that data augmentation can yield significant performance gains, with a larger training dataset leading to superior outcomes. Furthermore, the research examines the model's compression capabilities by counting the parameters in the neural network and by reducing the feature extractor's dimension. The authors also assess the model's inference speed by measuring the number of operations required per frame.

The dimer model, featuring directed and non-directed edges, is defined on a two-dimensional square lattice. When an Abelian gauge field with integer flux is introduced, the partition function of both the directed and non-directed variants can be expressed as a fermionic Pfaffian. In the thermodynamic limit, the free energy derived from these two models becomes identical regardless of the gauge field configuration, a result that holds true even without taking the flat flux limit. This phenomenon is interpreted as a classical statistical mechanical duality between the non-directed and directed versions, which corresponds to the modern anomaly inflow mechanism in Dirac fermions. Furthermore, this paper provides a detailed analysis of the Dirac Hamiltonian's spectrum, demonstrating that the spectrum of both models is the union of the zero mode spectrum and the non-zero mode spectrum of a "flat" Dirac operator. Additionally, it is shown that the non-zero mode contribution to the free energy vanishes in the thermodynamic limit, whereas the zero mode contribution is determined by the index of a Dirac operator. This operator acts on a spinor bundle with a charge defined by the statistical model and is situated in a line bundle with a connection whose curvature matches the flat flux. Ultimately, this work establishes a bridge between classical statistical mechanics and modern quantum field theory.

This study introduces a group lasso strategy designed to identify clusters of features within high-dimensional categorical datasets. By integrating group lasso with an embedding technique, the method facilitates the selection of specific feature categories. We evaluate the selection accuracy of the resulting groups and assess the model's performance on categorical outcomes. A comprehensive simulation framework tests various scenarios, including distinct levels of dimensionality, sample sizes, and levels of sparsity. Furthermore, we apply the method to a dataset concerning the identification of risk factors for dementia among older adults.

The rapid advancement of modern microprocessors with enhanced hardware virtualization capabilities has spurred renewed interest in hypervisors for mixed-criticality real-time systems. These architectures facilitate the isolated co-execution of applications with varying criticality levels, ensuring that high-priority software remains unaffected by lower-criticality tasks. This text introduces **T-Visor**, a Type-1 hypervisor built on the ARM Cortex-A series architecture, designed to deliver efficient and dependable execution for real-time workloads across different criticality tiers. T-Visor leverages advanced hardware virtualization features to create a streamlined hypervisor environment that supports multiple operating systems and enables seamless hardware-assisted context switching. Additionally, it implements comprehensive security and isolation mechanisms, including memory encryption, trusted execution environments, and trusted hardware roots. Evaluation results indicate that T-Visor offers superior performance and isolation compared to both non-virtualized bare-metal setups and software-based virtualization monitors.

This study addresses the panoramic stitching challenge under the assumption of a gravity-aligned camera. We introduce a novel framework that leverages a gravity prior to resolve ambiguities in feature matching and minimize camera exposure. By constraining camera poses to lie on a sphere with an equatorial plane perpendicular to the gravity vector, we establish a new optimization problem. We demonstrate that position estimation reduces to solving a quadratic form, which can be addressed via the power method, while angular estimation is reformulated as a polynomial optimization problem solvable using the Shrinkage approach. Comprehensive experiments on both stitched image datasets and those from real-world environments validate the effectiveness of our proposed method.

Chimera states are unique phenomena where coexisting synchronized and incoherent dynamics occur within identical coupled oscillator groups. This study investigates a specific configuration: two coupled groups with homogeneous internal connectivity but uniform heterogeneity applied across all units. We demonstrate that, contrary to systems lacking heterogeneity, introducing uniform variation enables the robust, tunable control of chimera characteristics such as the degree of partial synchrony and the oscillator frequencies in the incoherent group. Furthermore, we show that a significant degree of homogeneity is required to sustain chimeras; beyond a critical threshold of heterogeneity, these states vanish.

Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) offers a promising avenue for acquiring control skills in real-world scenarios by leveraging learned dynamics to simulate policies. However, these approaches often struggle with robustness when dealing with uncertainties stemming from unmodeled dynamics or environmental variables. This paper introduces a novel MBRL framework designed to address this lack of robustness by utilizing probabilistic model-based policy search. Unlike traditional methods that rely on point estimates, our uncertainty-aware strategy incorporates probabilistic outputs from the learned dynamics simulator. This allows for the propagation of uncertainty through to policy evaluation, enabling the selection of policies that remain effective across an array of probable scenarios. We validate this method on a variety of simulated environments, demonstrating that it surpasses both other uncertainty-aware MBRL techniques and standard non-robust baselines.

This work introduces higher slice algebras associated with quivers possessing a multi-layer structure. We establish that these higher slice algebras constitute a subcategory of the higher path algebras of the underlying quivers and maintain the property of being higher quasi-hereditary. Furthermore, we derive an explicit description of their higher Weyl algebras for the case of higher slice algebras linked to tilted algebras derived from extended cluster categories of type $A_n$.

The recent discovery of reflected entropy has offered a fresh avenue for investigating quantum entanglement within tensor networks. This study explores this concept using random tensor architectures. We demonstrate that in random tensor networks, reflected entropy adheres to the strong subadditivity condition. Furthermore, by applying the quantum reverse Shannon protocol, we establish an upper limit on randomized reflected entropy for these networks. Our findings indicate that random tensor networks can reach this maximum capacity, leading us to derive an explicit calculation for their reflected entropy. Additionally, we show that the variation of reflected entropy in these systems is governed by the same universal scaling laws found across many-body disordered quantum systems.

Although living cells are inherently noisy, they utilize diverse mechanisms to acquire and transmit information across generations. A primary focus is understanding how cells harness environmental stochasticity to generate heritable data. This study investigates noise-driven dynamics in systems featuring multiple positive feedback loops, which produce stable, self-sustained spatiotemporal patterns that endure for thousands of generations. Leveraging deep learning, we demonstrate that the initial configuration of these patterns reliably forecasts the subsequent gene expression profiles of the parent cell and its daughters. These findings indicate that the emergence and composition of these large-scale patterns serve as a robust readout of underlying cellular states, thereby facilitating the storage and inheritance of heritable information.

This study examines the dynamical behavior of a three-dimensional generalization of the Henon map. We demonstrate that when a third control parameter is introduced, new routes to chaos emerge, including period doubling, period doubling with one additional unstable direction, and chaotic saddle accumulation. We also explore how period windows arise from period doubling and how their boundaries are determined by saddle period-2 and period-4 cycles. Furthermore, we investigate how the distribution of chaotic saddles influences the formation of strange attractors.

This paper examines the distribution of hook lengths in Young diagrams within the subset divisible by two or three. Divisibility by two is addressed through a connection to the $q$-Catalan numbers, while the analysis for three relies on the generalized $q$-Catalan variant introduced by Garfinkle. We determine the exact average for the set of even hook lengths and, for the subset of hook lengths divisible by three, establish both the limiting average and its asymptotic behavior.

This tunneling time originates from contributions of both transmitted and reflected components of the wave function. We demonstrate that the magnitude of this tunneling time is determined by fluctuations of the spin within the transmitted part of the wave function. This analytical framework is validated by comparing it against the standard results for the constant potential barrier.

This work examines the distribution amplitudes for a $q\bar q$ P-wave nonrelativistic meson at the leading order. We demonstrate that these P‑wave distribution amplitudes are not independent; they are determined by the leading twist (DA) of the constituent quark and gluon fields. Consequently, the shape of the P‑wave distribution amplitudes is fixed by the assumption of a specific functional form for the corresponding leading twist objects. We evaluate the impact of quark and gluon spin and helicity decompositions on the resulting structure. Furthermore, we employ QCD sum rules to derive concrete P‑wave distribution amplitudes for the $J/\psi$ and $\eta_b$ mesons.

We present a proposal for constructing both single-qubit and two-qubit quantum gates utilizing a Bose-Einstein condensate. The scheme relies on the nonlinear photon propagation effects arising from Kerr media within the optical cavity framework. In this setup, the quantum bit is realized as a photonlike state of the cavity field, while nonlinear interactions between light and matter are driven by the Kerr-polarization contribution associated with a two-level system. We demonstrate that the resulting quantum gates are effectively implemented through the Kerr nonlinearity of a Bose-Feld-Hartree type condensate.

The asymptotic symmetries inherent in four-dimensional Minkowski space are demonstrated to correspond to the BMS algebra. We provide a derivation of the double soft theorem for gravitons, which, when expressed in a helicity basis, mirrors the structure of the BMS algebra. Crucially, this correspondence is mediated by a mapping to the spin-weight theory developed by Strominger and Edalatpanah. This equivalence allows us to establish the link between the two, yielding the "soft-BMS correspondence." Furthermore, we examine the connection between the BMS group and the Lorentz group, highlighting the role of the spin-charge hypothesis in relating the two. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of these findings for black hole physics.

Continual learning addresses a critical challenge in deep learning by enabling systems to acquire new competencies sequentially without compromising previously mastered skills. This framework mirrors human and animal learning, where experiences accumulate over time rather than being accessed simultaneously. A persistent obstacle remains the high failure rate associated with learning new tasks without forgetting old ones. To address this, we introduce an innovative approach called Neural Ensemble (NE), which integrates an online ensemble methodology with a dedicated memory buffer. NE functions by maintaining a set of specialized subnetworks, each dedicated to a specific task, and selectively activating the optimal subnetwork based on the incoming task identity. Furthermore, NE utilizes a shared backbone architecture to store a limited number of critical examples from past tasks, facilitating effective experience replay. Experimental evaluations on both synthetic and real-world benchmarks demonstrate that NE surpasses existing state-of-the-art continual learning techniques.

We introduce a new method for constructing metrics on manifolds equipped with generalized forms by leveraging dual pairs of such forms. We prove that when these generalized forms satisfy specific constraints, the resulting metric automatically becomes Ricci-flat. To demonstrate this, we examine generalized Kähler and Poisson structures, as well as holomorphic symplectic structures. In these cases, the metric derived from the structures is identical to the standard Kähler, symplectic, or more specific underlying metric. We further explore the implications of our construction in the context of RLH-structures and RLH-structures with torsion, highlighting the resulting parallelizations.

This paper focuses on permutation polynomials over the finite field $\mathbb{F}_{q^3}$. We analyze specific forms such as $x^r+ax^s$, $x^r+x^s$, $ax^r+x^s$, and $ax^r+x^s$, determining the conditions under which they are also complete permutation polovers $\mathbb{F}_{q^3}$.

Intestinal parasites are a significant global health issue, particularly in developing nations, necessitating a rapid and precise diagnostic approach. This study introduces a novel, automated classification method for intestinal parasite slides using a Deep Belief Network (DBN). The approach begins with the automatic segmentation of parasite cells from background elements via a deep convolutional neural network (CNN), followed by classification using an unsupervised DBN. The CNN's output serves as the DBN's input, where the latter learns latent features to determine the specific parasite class. Experimental results indicate strong performance with an accuracy of 96.66%, a recall rate of 96.66%, and an F1-score of 96.66%.

This study examines the optimal reinsurance and investment strategy within a jump-diffusion regime-switching financial framework. The objective is to minimize the joint value function for two players—an insurer and an investor—subject to an exponential utility function that accounts for both parties' risk preferences. This optimization problem is formulated as a non-zero-sum differential game characterized by a backward stochastic differential equation (BSDE) with a coupled system of equations featuring jump diffusion dynamics and regime-switching characteristics. To address this complex system, the work introduces a finite-dimensional approximation utilizing the finite difference method (FDM) to solve the equation system. The study further establishes the convergence of this FDM approximation toward the true value function of the original system. Finally, numerical simulations are provided to demonstrate the convergence of the approximation and to illustrate the joint influence of jumps and regime-switching dynamics on the optimal value function.

This study introduces a dual-action control architecture designed to enhance the flight performance of quadrotors. First, a dual-input rate feedback control loop manages the aircraft's attitude. Second, a feedforward trajectory controller, aimed at stabilizing and regulating flight paths over arbitrary trajectories, is implemented. To achieve this, stochastic dual simplex algorithms are employed to solve the model predictive control problem inherent to quadrotor dynamics. Additionally, a genetic filter estimates the aircraft's internal states. Simulation results demonstrate that this integrated control structure yields superior tracking accuracy and robustness against disturbances, such as wind gusts, when compared to a conventional gain-scheduled controller.

This article reviews low-energy pion-nucleon interactions, emphasizing the role chiral symmetry plays in governing the structure of nuclear forces. We examine how these interactions arise from the interplay between the nucleon and pion fields under the constraints of approximate chiral symmetry. Additionally, we discuss the implications of chiral effective field theory in modeling these phenomena and how it connects to experimental observables, reflecting the deep influence of symmetries on fundamental particle interactions.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) detector at the Large Hadron Collider (LHN) serves as a general-purpose instrument for the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tasked with analyzing proton-proton collisions at energies ranging from 7 to 13 TeV. Situated at the heart of CMS is its advanced silicon tracker, which is responsible for precisely measuring the impact parameters and momenta of charged particles produced in collisions. This critical role in identifying jets and discovering the Higgs boson and the top quark makes the system essential. The CMS tracker consists of three main components: a pixel detector, a transition radiation tracker, and a dual readout system. The most vital of these components, the pixel detector, is composed of four barrel sections and two end-cap disks. Designed to operate effectively even during the LHC's full high-luminosity running mode, it will be completely rebuilt to function at higher energies. This upgrade involves replacing existing technology with new, CM-stage 1 modules that feature dual readout capabilities. The pilot layer, specifically designed to precisely locate the primary interaction point, is a crucial component of this replacement plan. This article provides a detailed overview of the reconstruction software used for this pilot layer.

The Hyper Suprime-Cam Wide (HSC-SSP) survey is currently the largest ongoing wide-field survey in the Northern Hemisphere, designed to identify galaxies at redshifts $z<1$ for morphological classification. We present a machine-learning approach to distinguish between galaxies and active galactic nuclei (AGN) within the HSC-SSP catalog. We utilize the $r$-band images from HSC-SSP to create a sample of 1,000 galaxy hosts of luminous AGN, selected from the AGN catalog of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) and matched spatially to HSC-SSP sources. We then train a Random Forest classifier to classify these hosts as AGN versus galaxies, achieving an accuracy of 99.999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999

We investigate the phase-space density of short-range correlations (SRCs) within nuclei by analyzing high-energy electron-nucleus scattering data. Our findings indicate that the joint probability of finding a high-momentum nucleon alongside another nucleon with a lower relative momentum is significantly greater when the two nucleons occupy the same nuclear region. Furthermore, the correlation between these two momenta remains consistent across different types of nuclei.

The rapid growth of complex-valued deep learning has been fueled by its superior performance in specific applications, such as complex-valued convolutional neural networks and complex-valued transformers. However, these models have not yet matched the capabilities of their real-valued counterparts. This study introduces a new symmetry condition for complex-valued deep learning, which appears to be critical for achieving high performance. We demonstrate that the absence of this symmetry explains the performance gap between real and complex architectures. Furthermore, we propose a generalized framework for implementing co-domain symmetry, which enables complex-valued models to achieve performance on par with their real-valued equivalents.

We investigate the origins of elemental abundance variations in stars by analyzing a sample of 10 low-metallicity giants (Fe/H < -1.5) using high-resolution spectra. Our findings reveal significant scatter in elemental abundances, with magnitudes comparable to those observed in the Sun. To isolate these variations, we applied a rigorous selection process to ensure the study sample is free from non-abundance-related influences, specifically line-of-sight binary companions and magnetic fields. Consequently, these dispersions must originate from either intrinsic differences between the stars or from asymmetric mixing processes. Our results indicate that the dispersion is largely driven by intrinsic properties, particularly the initial helium fraction (Y), which accounts for most of the observed scatter in key elements like helium, carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen. However, we also conclude that asymmetric mixing processes play a secondary role in generating abundance variations.

This paper introduces a new toolbox designed to enhance machine learning (ML) applications within the social sciences by quantifying the sensitivity of model predictions to variations in feature values. The tool offers three distinct methods for evaluating this sensitivity, which are demonstrated through an application to financial literacy. In this specific case study, financial literacy is treated as a binary outcome, classified as either high or low. By calculating the partial derivative of the predicted probability with respect to each feature, the study identifies the minimum feature value adjustments required to shift the model's prediction from the lower to the upper class. The findings reveal that small incremental changes in credit scores and annual income are sufficient to alter classification outcomes, whereas significant adjustments in age, income volatility, and financial knowledge levels are necessary to produce similar effects.

Quantum machine learning (QML) is a rapidly developing field that explores the use of quantum algorithms for data analysis. While numerous classical and quantum classification algorithms exist, most current quantum models depend on NISQ (Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum) hardware requiring specific ansatz circuits for training. This study introduces a novel classification approach utilizing a Superconducting qUId for detecting linearly separable patterns. Our method employs a single-qubit system where a parameterized rotation angle serves as the ansatz. We demonstrate that this SQUID-based scheme achieves higher accuracy than state-of-the-art alternatives, including Variational Classification Algorithms (VCA), and can be executed efficiently on existing NISQ processors.

The PALE-OCENE framework introduces a novel approach to the passive detection of low-energy nuclear recoils by utilizing defects created in diamond through electron-beam irradiation. These defects, known as color centers, serve as the sensing units. Utilizing density functional theory and the calculation of defect properties via the tight-binding approximation, the study identifies a specific configuration: a single substitutional nitrogen atom paired with an adjacent vacancy in nitrogen-doped cubic boron nitride. This configuration is named the "boron nitride nitride-vacancy color center" (BN-NV). The research demonstrates that the BN-NV exhibits favorable characteristics for passive detection tasks, including low thresholds for detecting both Leonard and MeV-scale Ge nuclear recoils, and maintains these sensitivities even when the material is doped with boron. Furthermore, theoretical analysis indicates that the BN-NV is more effective than the conventional nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond for these specific passive applications.

We investigate the dynamics of active colloidal dimers undergoing spontaneous polarization when placed within activity gradient fields. Our findings indicate that the direction of the induced polarization is dictated by the specific geometry of the molecular components. We propose a simplified effective particle model to account for the observed behaviors, a framework that successfully captures the mechanisms behind self-propulsion, gradient polarization, and stable orbital trajectories. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the direction of these orbital motions is contingent upon the sign of the Darcy flow induced by the difference in activity between the two constituent particles. These insights offer a new approach for engineering autonomous molecular systems capable of navigation within activity-laden fluids.

"This study examines multiple magnetoroton excitations within fractional quantum Hall systems by analyzing the finite momentum limit of the dynamic structure factor, $S(q,\omega)$. We establish exact sum rules for $S(q,\omega)$ and demonstrate that, in the large magnetic field limit where $q \to 0$, the first sum rule converges to the total energy spectrum of magnetrarotons, while the second integral yields the square of the magnetorotron effective mass. Furthermore, we evaluate the sum-rule constraints for $S(q,\omega)$ within the Laughlin model and compare these theoretical predictions against the numerical results reported by Jain and Patel [Phys. Rev. B 46, 10023 (1992)]."

Clustering is a fundamental feature of numerous real-world networks, including social and contact networks. This study examines clustering within the framework of Contagious Diseases using a geometric model, where edges are determined by the proximity of nodes in a latent metric space. We demonstrate that when networks exhibit strong clustering, epidemic spread is significantly restricted compared to scenarios without it. Furthermore, we establish that as the network size approaches infinity, the threshold for disease invasion remains unaffected by edge probabilities, provided these probabilities diminish sufficiently fast. These insights are supported by numerical simulations, which also reveal that clustering can reduce the final prevalence of an epidemic by up to 50%.

This study examines the maximum likelihood estimation of CMB maps in the presence of point sources, highlighting that the standard Gaussian likelihood method generates artificial "X'-shaped" artifacts at the locations of these sources. We demonstrate that these artifacts stem from the non-invertibility of the pixel-to-arcminute smoothing kernels, which are typically modeled as modified Gaussian functions. To resolve this issue, we propose implementing a modified modified Gaussian kernel with a cut-off, ensuring invertibility. We further show that the choice of this cut-off parameter is critical for minimizing map artifacts. Additionally, we suggest an optimal strategy for handling point sources, which involves masking them prior to mapmaking and then subtracting their contribution using a best-fit model.

"Visualizing instructions is a promising strategy to mitigate reference ambiguity in language-guided reinforcement learning. However, current methods often fail to generalize to objects introduced later in the task sequence. This study investigates the generalization of spatial references by comparing two visualization approaches: static images and animated videos. Our analysis reveals that while static images lead to better sample efficiency, they exhibit lower fidelity in the final episodes. Conversely, videos demonstrate the ability to generalize to unreferenced objects. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the superior performance of static images stems from their lower data complexity, which allows the agent to learn the rules for dynamic references more effectively. Ultimately, these results indicate that dynamic visualizations are particularly effective for teaching spatial dynamics to agents."

Quantum process tomography is a fundamental technique for characterizing the complete behavior of a quantum process. While standard methods typically require many copies of an output state, the concept of a shadow process allows for the characterization of an entire process using a single copy. We introduce shadow process tomography, which extends the well-established shadow state tomography to handle quantum channels. Our approach demonstrates that shadow process tomography can be implemented via a shadow state tomography protocol, thereby leveraging existing experimental advancements. We further establish a theoretical bound on the sample complexity required for this task. Furthermore, we outline practical protocols for both qubit channels and more general $N$-dimensional channels, showing that the task can be realized using a fixed number of measurements that do not scale with the dimension of the input state.

This study establishes precise bounds on the Cheeger constant for convex domains in two dimensions, surpassing previous results by J. L. Marstrand and R. Kershaw. Additionally, we present a more stringent lower bound specifically for convex polygons. Our approach relies on a geometric analysis of level sets derived from distance functions.

This study addresses the challenge of optimizing communication trajectory for UAVs within time-constrained scenarios. The primary objective is to maximize the minimum data rate experienced by a set of ground users, subject to a total flight time limit and a requirement to maintain a specific coverage area. To solve this, the authors propose a new trajectory optimization method that incorporates practical constraints, including maximum speed, minimum curvature, and maximum power output. The resulting optimization problem is classified as non-convex; however, it is converted into an equivalent convex form using second-order cone programming (SOCP). The effectiveness of the proposed solution is validated through numerical simulations, which also explore the impact of various parameters on system performance.

We examine bilayer graphene with Coulomb interactions using a renormalization group framework. Our findings indicate that the system becomes unstable toward a gapless symmetry-breaking metallic phase, characterized by a specific ordering of electron spins and lattice spins alongside the spontaneous breaking of layer symmetry. This instability arises from a combination of interlayer Coulomb interactions and the unique momentum structure of the bare vertex. Our analysis employs the functional renormalization group, which offers a more comprehensive exploration of the fixed point landscape compared to previous studies relying solely on the Hubbard model.

The thermal evolution of the conformation of the endofullerene Sc₂TbN@C₈₀ was examined on an h-BN/Ni(111) substrate using a combination of temperature-controlled low-energy electron diffraction (LEED), scanning tunneling microscopy (STM), and density functional theory (DFT). The study reveals that heating the sample from 100 K to 300 K triggers a structural phase transition from the p2mm to the c2mm symmetry. Furthermore, LEED analysis indicates that Sc₂TbN@C₈₀ adopts a c2mm arrangement specifically at 300 K.

The Internet of Things (IoT) is rapidly expanding, connecting billions of low-power devices that communicate via the internet. These devices are characterized by their small size, limited computational resources, and minimal energy consumption capabilities. As security vulnerabilities in IoT devices have become increasingly apparent, there is an urgent need to develop robust and secure protocols specifically designed for these constrained environments. This study evaluates various ciphers and key exchange mechanisms suitable for the low-powered IoT architecture. The analysis reveals that ciphers utilizing the Galois Field (GF)(2^8), including AES-128 and ChaCha20, offer superior security; however, their resource demands exceed those available on many IoT platforms. Consequently, these devices require lighter alternatives. This paper analyzes several lightweight ciphers and key exchange methods tailored to these constraints, ultimately recommending the 128-bit PRESENT cipher combined with the Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman key exchange as the most effective solution.

This study introduces a novel experimental design for the Ramsey sequence, specifically tailored for magnetometry. By leveraging Bayesian optimization, the approach minimizes the total cost function defined as the sum of measurement durations and the associated squared uncertainty regarding the magnetic field. This framework allows for the optimization of both the free precession time and the count of a full Larmor rotation cycles. The method's efficacy is validated through simulations of a spin-1/2 particle subjected to a constant magnetic field and a stochastic linear noise component. The results demonstrate that the proposed strategy significantly outperforms a standard Ramsey protocol, achieving a substantial reduction in parameter uncertainty.

We introduce a multi-scale network centrality metric rooted in Gromov hyperbolicity, leveraging the triangle inequality excess to determine centrality based on the degree of network hyperbolicity via geodesic distances. This approach contrasts with traditional centrality measures, which typically rely on local attributes like node degree or immediate neighbors. By utilizing the global hyperbolicity excess, our method captures a network's overall structure. We demonstrate that this metric is robust and stable, maintaining consistent results despite variations in network topology, the removal of nodes, or fluctuations in edge weights. Furthermore, we show that it possesses high predictive power in forecasting the spread of epidemics and exhibits strong positive correlations with both human centrality and social influence.

This work introduces a new gravitational theory based on azimuthal symmetry, which utilizes a four-dimensional manifold and four scalar potentials. It establishes four field equations derived from the variation of a proposed action. The theory's structure is notably simple, allowing for the explicit calculation of the metric tensor components. Specifically, it is demonstrated that the newly formulated metric matches the metric of General Relativity in all solutions that are spherically symmetric.

We demonstrate that within these two categories, any two bundles are strictly equivalent if and only if they share the same dimension for each form block's count. Furthermore, we establish the existence of two distinct equivalence classes for matrix pencil bundles when considered under strict equivalence but not equivalence in strict form structure.

This study establishes that for strongly monotone discrete-time dynamical systems with smooth mappings, the generic long-term behavior aligns with the standard model of hyperbolic dynamics featuring a finite collection of basic, non-degenerate attractors and repellers, alongside a repulsive remainder set. We demonstrate that the strongly monotone assumption enables a significantly streamlined proof of this result by leveraging the well-developed theory of $C^0$ monotone systems, rather than relying exclusively on smoothness. This approach underscores the significance of invariance under $C^0$ perturbations when characterizing asymptotic dynamics and suggests that strong monotonicity may be overly restrictive; it likely suffices merely to be robustly open, a condition naturally met by conditions ensuring loss of mass in probabilistic models. Applying these insights to such a condition within the context of invariance measures leads to the conclusion that the resulting measure is unique, absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure on the probability space, and possesses a positive, unique, and continuous spectrum.

Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) serves as a primary method for determining the ground state of Hamiltonians on near-term quantum hardware. However, the approach typically relies on an iterative cycle between quantum and classical components to minimize the variational energy, a process often hindered by the high computational cost of classical optimization and the difficulty in selecting an appropriate initial ansatz state. This paper introduces a novel adaptive VQE strategy that leverages qubit-excitation operators to facilitate the computation of the anti-commutator between Hamiltonian terms and the ansatz state within the quantum processor. By shifting the evaluation of this critical anti-commutator term from the classical realm to the quantum processor, the proposed method eliminates the bottleneck associated with heavy classical optimization. Furthermore, it allows for the flexible use of various ansätze, including those that are easy to prepare but otherwise challenging to handle. The efficacy of this new protocol is validated through numerical simulations applied to the variational calculation of electronic structures.

Deep generative models, such as Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) and Energy-based models (EBMs), are typically trained using stochastic gradient descent with stochastic samples from the posterior or uniform prior. This work introduces a new training strategy for these frameworks by utilizing maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimates for latent variables and/or samples, rather than drawing random instances. We demonstrate that this approach yields several distinct benefits: (1) it enables the direct optimization of the exact log-likelihood, (2) it facilitates the training of models that are intractable under the standard variational inference procedure, and (3) it produces superior samples and generative capabilities. The method is empirically validated on established Energy-based models and VAEs using the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, with results showing marked improvements over conventional variational techniques.

The Hubble tension has reignited interest in the future of cosmology, with the detection of a stochastic gravitational wave background (SGWB) by NANOGrav potentially offering a transformative opportunity. This paper investigates the SGWB arising from primordial fluctuations amplified by a stiff equation of state ($w=0$) during the early universe. Such a background would peak in the nanohertz to millihertz range, exhibiting a spectral index of $\alpha=-2/3$. This signal could be observed by NANOGrav, the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (Virgo), and the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA), although it would also be detectable by pulsar timing arrays and space-based interferometers. If confirmed, this SGWB would resolve the Hubble tension and provide a compelling explanation for NANOGrav's data. Furthermore, this amplified SGWB would offer a novel test for the primordial origin of gravitational waves and could yield insights into the nature of dark matter.

We report the first high-resolution ALMA Atacama Compact Array (ACA) observations of the gas-rich comet C/2015 ER61 (PanSTARRS) at a distance of 1.1 AU. The data, acquired in May 2015, utilized a 79-channel ACA array operating at 89 GHz to map CS (J=2-1) emission. Our analysis of the angular power spectrum reveals a significant deviation from the typical point-source behavior seen in cometary outflows, instead indicating a spatially extended emission structure. This extended structure is consistent with a distributed source of CS, offering a new perspective on the production mechanisms of this molecule. Furthermore, our study demonstrates the ACA's potential utility for investigating the spatial distribution of cometary gases.

This study presents an unsupervised speech synthesis framework that is both straightforward and effective. We propose a text-to-speech system that leverages speech-to-speech translation alongside self-supervised learning to convert raw audio into parameterized speech, which is subsequently converted into text-tuned speech through a neural text-totextive approach. We also present a new unsupervised method for estimating prosody using self-supervised learning. Experiments demonstrate that our unsupervised system achieves performance comparable to best-in-class supervised models. Additionally, our unsupervised method for estimating pitch achieves results that are on par with the most advanced techniques.
